explain.headline: Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench May Close Legislative Privilege vs Free Speech Case
static: Legislative privileges are special rights and immunities enjoyed by houses of Parliament and state legislatures, and their members, to enable them to function effectively.
Article 105 of the Constitution deals with the powers and privileges of Parliament, while Article 194 deals with the powers and privileges of state legislatures and their members.
In India, legislative privileges are not explicitly codified into a comprehensive single statute, and largely trace their roots to the practices of the British House of Commons.

When legislative privilege conflicts with fundamental rights like freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a), the judiciary examines the boundaries to ensure fundamental rights are not unduly overridden.
explain.what: The Supreme Court's seven-judge bench is set to dispose of a long-standing case regarding legislative privilege versus free speech after learning the underlying assembly resolution was withdrawn.

explain.background: Legislative privileges under Articles 105 and 194 often create legal tensions when exercised against fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and expression.

Demonstrates how courts handle matters that have become legally academic over time.
Reflects judicial efforts to clear pendency involving decades-old constitutional questions.

The resolution imposed a 15-day sentence on journalists including editors N Ravi and S Selvam.
The Tamil Nadu assembly withdrew the resolution in the year 2004.
The bench handling the matter is led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.

points: A seven-judge Supreme Court bench is scheduled to hear a long-pending case regarding legislative privilege versus free speech.
The case stems from a 2003 Tamil Nadu assembly breach of privilege resolution that imposed a 15-day sentence on certain journalists.
Senior counsel representing the Tamil Nadu assembly informed the court that the assembly withdrew the resolution in 2004.
Counsel argued that the cause of action for the writ petition no longer survives and the issue has become academic.
The bench, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, indicated it would take the 2004 resolution on record and dispose of the petitions.
The original petitions were filed by N Ravi and S Selvam, who were then editors of 'The Hindu' and 'Murasoli' newspapers respectively.
Arrest warrants were initially issued against the editors and journalists following the November 7, 2003 assembly resolution.
The Supreme Court had stayed the arrests of the journalists nearly 23 years ago before the upcoming hearing to close the matter.

The Delhi High Court had ruled that law students should not be barred from exams or academic progression due to poor attendance records.
The Bar Council of India and prominent law schools challenged the verdict, arguing that eroding compulsory attendance harms academic discipline and institutional independence.

The High Court had also ordered the BCI to review mandatory attendance norms for LLB courses to avoid causing mental stress to students.

points: A collaborative scientific study by IMD, NCMRWF, and Atria University evaluated five decades of empirical data from 1971 to 2022 to assess climate extremes.
The study synthesized seven atmospheric and hydrological variables into a consolidated metric known as the India Climate Extremes Index.
Climate change in India is highly heterogeneous, with different geographical regions facing distinct, compounding extreme events rather than uniform temperature rises.
Land area exposed to extreme temperatures in central and north-western India expanded by 20% to 40% per decade between 1971 and 2022.
South India is desiccating rapidly with over 40% of the eastern coastal belt across Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu facing recurring droughts.
The north-eastern region shows high hydro-climatic volatility, marked by short-duration cloudbursts alternating with unseasonal dry spells.
Climate extremes heavily impact agriculture through terminal heat stress on rabi crops, peninsular rainfed farming vulnerabilities, and livestock metabolic stress.
Socio-economic impacts include reduced outdoor labor work capacity, increased vector-borne diseases, distress migration, climateflation, and sub-national fiscal divergence.
India has responded through frameworks like the NAPCC, revamped SAPCC 2.0, NAFCC, and expanded municipal Heat Action Plans.

static: The Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan were launched in 2017 by Russia, India, China, Iran, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, with Central Asian Republics joining later.
It serves as a regional platform for deliberating on stability, economic progress, and security matters concerning Afghanistan.
The format has evolved alongside the shifting political reality in Afghanistan, transitioning from excluding the Taliban initially to engaging them and eventually granting them full participation.

Regional powers like Russia and China have increasingly pursued pragmatic, interest-led engagements with the Taliban, prioritizing counter-terrorism and connectivity over values-based conditionalities.

significance: Highlights the growing friction between regional actors like Pakistan and the Taliban regime over cross-border security and terrorism.
Demonstrates how major regional powers are dropping human rights and inclusive governance from diplomatic agendas in favor of pragmatic counter-terrorism cooperation.
Exposes the limitations of existing regional tracks in addressing the core political and humanitarian rights of Afghan citizens.
prelims: The eighth edition of the Moscow Format Consultations concluded in the Russian capital on Monday.
Egypt and Belarus attended the eighth edition as guests.

points: The eighth edition of the Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan concluded in Moscow with multiple regional nations participating, but failed to issue a joint statement for the first time.
Tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan prevented consensus, as Pakistan accused the Taliban regime of complicity in terrorism while the Taliban objected.
Russia regretted the outcome but stated the format would continue to function even without a final document.

Past iterations of the Moscow Format focused on urging the Taliban to form an inclusive government and protect human rights, but references to inclusive governance were dropped by the seventh iteration.
In July 2025, Moscow granted formal recognition to the Taliban government, and the Taliban participated in the current format as a full member.
Participants prioritize counter-terrorism, trade, and connectivity, viewing the Taliban as a partner against groups like the Islamic State – Khorasan Province (ISKP).
Consistently, statements from the format have opposed US actions, criticizing the 20-year military presence, warning against foreign military infrastructure, and opposing politicization of aid.
Meanwhile, the Cambridge Afghanistan Series Conference released the Cambridge Declaration, charting principles for democratic cooperation, women's rights, and an Afghan-led political process.

points: Belgian-born scientist Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in physics for his efforts to demystify a rare group of cosmic neutrinos.
Halzen first published about cosmic neutrinos in 2013 and spent his career trying to prove that neutrino astronomy is possible.
Neutrinos are tiny cosmic particles with no electric charge and extraordinarily small mass, making them extremely difficult to detect.
Halzen had the original idea to turn the vast Antarctic ice into a giant particle detector to catch neutrino collisions.
His work was instrumental to constructing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, which glimpsed the first high-energy neutrinos from faraway galaxies.
Sensors at the observatory are buried about 8,200 feet deep in transparent Antarctic ice to protect against interference from cosmic rays and radiation.
The research team must painstakingly differentiate cosmic neutrinos from atmospheric neutrinos, detecting thousands of charged particles every second to find rare signals.
The IceCube observatory involves more than 400 scientists across 14 countries and is supported by the National Science Foundation.

static: The Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 governs the appointment process of top poll panels.

A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court requires a minimum of five judges under Article 145(3) of the Constitution to interpret substantial questions of law.

static: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India's central banking institution, established on April 1, 1935, under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
The Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934 lists scheduled banks that meet specific criteria regarding paid-up capital, reserves, and depositor protection.
Scheduled banks enjoy certain privileges, such as the right to borrow funds from the RBI on repo rates and participation in clearing house operations.
Payments banks are a differentiated bank model in India intended to widen financial inclusion by offering small savings accounts and remittance services without credit risk.

explain.background: Scheduled banks under the RBI Act enjoy special privileges, whereas Paytm Payments Bank faced regulatory cancellation of its licence and subsequent liquidation.
significance: Marks a major regulatory intervention against a major digital payments bank over non-compliance and depositor risks.

prelims: Paytm Payments Bank Limited was excluded from the Second Schedule vide Notification dated July 31, 2026.

points: The Reserve Bank of India has excluded Paytm Payments Bank Limited from the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

The Delhi High Court appointed former SBI Chief General Manager Girikumar M Nair as the Official Liquidator for the winding up process.

explain.headline: New species of extinct crocodilian, similar to North India's gharial, discovered in Egypt
static: Gharials (Gavialis gangeticus) are freshwater crocodilians native to the Indian subcontinent, easily recognized by their long, thin snouts adapted for catching fish.
The species is currently classified as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List, primarily threatened by river damming, sand mining, and pollution.

The Eocene epoch, spanning from about 56 to 33.9 million years ago, was a period of global warmth supporting diverse marine and terrestrial reptiles.

explain.why_in_news: The discovery was published by an international research team in the Royal Society Open Science journal on October 7, 2026.
explain.background: Fossil evidence indicates that gharials once had a global distribution over 100 million years before eventually disappearing from the Mediterranean region around six million years ago.
significance: Provides new insights into gavialoid diversity and prehistoric distribution across the Mediterranean region.
Demonstrates the power of modern computed tomography in reclassifying historical fossil collections.
Highlights how historical climate and sea level changes altered prehistoric reptilian biodiversity over millions of years.
prelims: The new extinct crocodile species is named Herugavialis cairensis.
The fossils were found in the 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation in Egypt.

The study was published in the Royal Society Open Science journal.

The newly identified animal is similar to the modern gharial found in the rivers of North India.
Researchers used computed tomography to examine the inside of a fossilized skull originally found in the 1920s.
The fossils were previously thought to belong to the genus Tomistoma, but new analysis established it as a distinct, unknown species.
The new species was named Herugavialis cairensis after the Egyptian god Heru due to its Sphinx-like missing snout tip.
At least two other gharial species lived in the shallow marine environments covering ancient Egypt around 45 million years ago.
All crocodiles ultimately disappeared from the Mediterranean region around six million years ago due to changing global temperatures and sea levels.
The study was published in the Royal Society Open Science journal on October 7, 2026, by an international team of researchers.

static: The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health, established on 7 April 1948.
Childhood obesity is a major public health challenge globally, linked to changing dietary patterns, sedentary lifestyles, and urban environments.
Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancers are major causes of mortality worldwide and are increasingly linked to early-life obesity.
Systemic public health measures for tackling obesity include front-of-pack labeling, taxation on sugar-sweetened beverages, and promoting physical education in schools.

explain.background: Childhood obesity has surged globally over the past few decades, prompting health bodies to formulate evidence-based treatment and prevention protocols.
significance: Provides a standardized global framework for clinicians and policymakers to address the rising epidemic of youth obesity.
Helps prevent long-term noncommunicable diseases such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular conditions in adulthood.
Highlights the critical link between mental health support and chronic disease management in young demographics.
prelims: Child and adolescent obesity has quadrupled since 1990, rising from two to eight per cent in the five-to-19 age group.
In 2024, there were around 170 million children and adolescents living with obesity globally.
WHO does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery, or weight-loss devices for children aged 0-9 years.
GLP-1 therapies are mentioned as approved medicines for adolescents aged 10-19 under strict conditions.
explain.mains: Examine the public health implications of rising childhood obesity rates globally and discuss the efficacy of the recent WHO guidelines in addressing this crisis.
explain.who: World Health Organization (WHO), Dr. Luz María De Regil
explain.video_query: WHO first global guidelines on child obesity explained

stories.ai_why: First global guidelines on child obesity by WHO matter for public health.

points: Child and adolescent obesity has quadrupled since 1990, rising from two per cent to around eight per cent among youngsters aged five to 19.
In 2024, approximately 170 million children and adolescents were living with obesity, including 70 million aged five to nine and 100 million adolescents.
The WHO defines obesity as a chronic, relapsing disease triggered by excessive fat deposits that can be managed through effective care.
Obesity raises the risk of noncommunicable diseases like type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, alongside severe social stigma and mental health issues.
WHO strongly recommends dietary changes, physical activity, and behaviour-changing interventions for young people.
For children aged 0-9 years, the WHO does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery, or weight-loss devices.
For adolescents aged 10-19 years, approved medicines like GLP-1 therapies or bariatric surgery are considered only under strict conditions when lifestyle programs fail.
WHO emphasizes addressing mental health alongside obesity and calls for systemic policies making healthy diets and physical activity more accessible and affordable.

The Andhra Pradesh Policy for Promotion of Foreign Higher Educational Institutions (FHEIs) and Private Universities, 2026 aims to facilitate campus establishments without state financial burden.
The policy seeks to promote international academic partnerships, research, and innovation while giving students access to global-standard education locally.

static: India operates under a Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework enshrined in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

Section 45ZB of the amended RBI Act, 1934 provides for an empowered six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) constituted by the Central Government in 2016.

Poses challenges for borrowers through higher EMIs while offering marginal relief to savers through increased deposit rates.

The core issue is balancing inflation control through higher borrowing costs against maintaining sustainable economic growth amidst domestic and global uncertainties.
Retail inflation reached 4.82% in August, driven by rising food prices, weather disruptions, and drought concerns affecting agricultural output.
Global pressures include a crude oil price surge past $100 per barrel, geopolitical tensions in West Asia, and the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.
External financial pressures stem from elevated US interest rates, higher US yields, and foreign investment outflows triggering currency pressures.
Domestic agricultural risks involve potential El Niño conditions extending into 2027 and reservoir levels dropping about 20% below the previous year.
The RBI revised its FY27 GDP growth projection upwards from 6.7% to 7.1% despite the tighter monetary policy stance.
The policy aims to contain inflation, anchor inflation expectations, manage external pressures, and prevent price increases from becoming entrenched.

static: India is recognized as one of the 17 mega-diverse countries globally, containing four designated biodiversity hotspots: the Western Ghats, the Himalayas, the Indo-Burma region, and Sundaland.

The Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats (IDWH) is a centrally sponsored scheme of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change providing financial assistance for protected areas and species recovery.

Emphasizes the urgent need to address data deficits and fund neglected micro-habitats and non-flagship species.

points: India sustains nearly 8 percent of global flora and 7.5 percent of fauna across four global biodiversity hotspots, with high endemism and over a thousand species categorized as threatened.
Targeted conservation frameworks like the National Red List Roadmap aim to produce National Red Data Books by 2030 to bridge the data deficit where only 7.2 percent of fauna is assessed.
Species recovery programs funded by the Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats scheme support recovery across 24 critically endangered wildlife species.
Asiatic lion populations in Gir expanded to 891 by 2025, and Madhya Pradesh recorded 12,981 vultures in 2025 due to conservation breeding and a veterinary diclofenac ban.
Surveys under Project Nilgiri Tahr recorded a rise to 1,364 individuals, and Palk Bay's Dugong Conservation Reserve registered a baseline of 270 sea cows.
Challenges persist due to a charismatic megafauna bias leaving non-flagship species underfunded, linear infrastructure causing mortality, and ecological assessment gaps.
Proposals include institutionalizing decentralized non-lapsing conservation funds, leveraging global blended finance, and accelerating the 2030 Red List Roadmaps.
Sustaining ecological gains requires protecting vulnerable micro-habitats, grasslands, and marine meadows alongside empowering grassroots communities.

points: India's urban centres face rising demands for infrastructure and public services due to rapid urbanisation and ageing infrastructure.
Property tax is the most important own-source revenue of municipal bodies, yet India's cumulative property tax is only 0.15-0.2 percent of GDP.
Property taxation involves three stages: enumeration, valuation and assessment, and billing and collection, with weaknesses at each stage.
Incomplete property enumeration, outdated records, and manual record-keeping reduce the accuracy of the tax base and limit municipal revenues.
Most municipalities use an area-based valuation using a base rate per square foot per month rather than linking tax to current market values.
Municipal base rates are revised infrequently compared with circle rates, leading to weak tax buoyancy and limited responsiveness of revenues.
Excessive exemptions for government properties and religious institutions further narrow the tax base and reduce municipal revenue collections.
Shortages of municipal staff, irregular municipal elections, and poor financial reporting severely limit effective property tax assessment and collection.
Structural reforms require strengthening human resources, combining technology with physical verification, rationalising exemptions, and ensuring timely municipal elections.

points: The Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent, marking the first rate increase since February 2023.

The core issue is how higher borrowing costs affect household budgets, business financing, bond prices, and overall credit demand.
For floating-rate home loan borrowers, a 25 bps hike can either raise monthly EMIs or extend loan tenures, increasing cumulative interest burdens.
Taking a ₹50 lakh home loan at 7.5 percent for 25 years could see EMIs rise by roughly ₹800 per month, adding about ₹2.4 lakh over the full tenure.
Companies dependent on debt, especially in interest-rate-sensitive sectors like real estate and automobiles, may face higher financing costs and pressure.
Savers could benefit as banks gradually reprice fixed deposits, while existing long-duration debt funds face price pressure because bond prices move inversely to yields.
Experts advise that the broader signal of a tightening cycle matters more for borrowers and investors than the immediate 25 bps hike alone.

points: The Supreme Court agreed to examine an application seeking the recall of its September 23 split verdict regarding the 2023 law governing Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioner appointments.
The recall application was mentioned before Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana by Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan.

The core issue revolves around whether challenges to the 2023 law should be referred to a larger Constitution Bench, which led to divergent views between Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma.
Justice Dipankar Datta held that a larger-bench reference was not necessary, whereas Justice Sharma favoured such a reference, resulting in the split verdict.
The recall plea raises a concern regarding a possible apprehension of bias involving Justice Sharma because his son serves as a standing counsel for the Election Commission of India.
The underlying dispute challenges the 2023 law for altering the selection panel composition by excluding the Chief Justice of India.
A separate curative petition has also been filed by another party against the split verdict to follow its own legal process.
The CJI will decide whether the recall application is maintainable and if the split verdict should be reconsidered by an appropriate larger bench.

explain.headline: Supreme Court Directs Centre to Form Committee on Unethical Pharma Marketing Practices
static: The Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP) is a set of guidelines issued by the government to regulate promotional activities and interactions between drug companies and healthcare professionals.
Under Indian regulations, medical ethics and professional conduct for doctors are primarily overseen by the National Medical Commission (NMC) through its regulations.
Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which the judiciary interprets to include the right to health and access to safe healthcare.
The Apex Laboratories case (2022) is a landmark Supreme Court judgment holding that freebies given to doctors by pharma companies are not business expenditures deductible under income tax law.

The Department of Pharmaceuticals, operating under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, formulates and implements policies relating to the promotion and development of the pharmaceutical industry in India.
explain.what: The Supreme Court directed the Union government to set up a three-member committee to evaluate the necessity of statutory regulations to curb unethical pharmaceutical marketing practices and doctor-pharma interactions.
explain.why_in_news: The order was issued during the hearing of a petition pointing out the lack of statutory penalties for pharmaceutical companies that offer freebies and inducements to doctors.
explain.background: The judiciary frequently examines public health concerns regarding pharma-doctor relationships, referencing previous judgments like Apex Laboratories and existing voluntary codes like the UCPMP.
significance: Addresses regulatory gaps between penalizing doctors versus penalizing pharmaceutical companies for unethical marketing.
Reinforces the constitutional right to health under Article 21 by emphasizing effective enforcement of public health standards.
Highlights the judicial doctrine of separation of powers while ensuring executive accountability in policy formulation.
prelims: The Supreme Court bench was composed of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta.
The newly ordered committee is a three-member body.
The committee is expected to submit its report within two months of its first meeting.
The matter was listed for consideration of the compliance affidavit on January 29, 2027.
explain.mains: Examine the regulatory gaps in curbing unethical pharmaceutical marketing practices in India. Discuss the need for a statutory framework to govern the relationship between pharmaceutical companies and medical practitioners.
explain.who: Supreme Court, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, Justice Vikram Nath, Justice Sandeep Mehta
explain.video_query: Supreme Court committee on unethical pharma marketing practices explained

stories.ai_why: Supreme Court directive on unethical pharma practices and regulations.

points: The Supreme Court directed the Union government to form a three-member committee to examine whether statutory regulations are needed to curb unethical pharma marketing practices.

The bench comprising Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta passed the order while hearing a petition seeking legally enforceable rules governing pharma marketing and doctor-company interactions.

The core issue debated is the imbalance where doctors face penalties for accepting freebies under existing rules, while pharmaceutical companies offering such inducements lack direct statutory penalties.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta informed the Court that the Centre agreed to set up the committee following inter-departmental discussions between the Departments of Pharmaceuticals, Health, and Legal Affairs.
The existing framework includes the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices, 2024, which will continue to govern practices in the interim.
Petitioners questioned the new committee, noting a high-level committee was already promised in a 2022 affidavit, and argued that voluntary codes fail to prevent undue influence on prescriptions.
The Supreme Court observed that a regulatory framework's efficacy must be judged by its implementation and enforcement rather than just the mere existence of norms.
Recognizing the separation of powers, the Court stated it cannot substitute executive policy determination but must ensure the framework aligns with constitutional guarantees and Article 21.
The committee must submit its report within two months of its first meeting, and the Centre must file a compliance affidavit by January 29, 2027.

explain.headline: Living Planet Report 2026: WWF and ZSL Release Global Biodiversity Assessment
static: The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) is an international non-governmental organization founded in 1961, working in the field of wilderness preservation and the reduction of human impact on the environment.
The Zoological Society of London (ZSL) is an international conservation charity that works to restore wildlife and manages the Living Planet Index in partnership with WWF.
The Living Planet Index (LPI) measures relative population abundance of vertebrate species from terrestrial, freshwater, and marine habitats globally from a baseline year of 1970.
The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) sets out four goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030 to halt and reverse biodiversity loss.
India is one of 17 megadiverse countries, harboring nearly 8 percent of global flora and 7.5 percent of global fauna on roughly 2.4 percent of the world's land area.
explain.what: The Living Planet Report 2026 revealed a 73.2 percent average decline in monitored global vertebrate populations from 1970 to 2022, while emphasizing critical pathways for systemic transformation before 2030.
explain.why_in_news: The report was recently published biennially by the WWF and the Zoological Society of London.
explain.background: The Living Planet Report tracks global biodiversity trends and vertebrate populations using the Living Planet Index to guide international conservation policies.
significance: Highlights the severe economic and ecological risks associated with widespread biodiversity degradation and ecosystem collapse.
Provides vital metrics for tracking progress towards global targets like the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and SDGs 14 and 15.
Showcases India's unique conservation successes in reviving flagship species like tigers, lions, rhinos, and vultures as a replicable global model.
prelims: Monitored wildlife populations fell by an average of 73.2% between 1970 and 2022.
Freshwater ecosystems suffered the steepest collapse at 85%.
Latin America and the Caribbean recorded the steepest regional decline of 95%.
India's wild tiger population reached 3,682 according to recent census data, accounting for over 75% of the global total.
explain.mains: Analyze the major findings of the Living Planet Report 2026 and discuss India's initiatives in reversing biodiversity decline through community participation and targeted conservation.
explain.who: WWF and Zoological Society of London
explain.video_query: Living Planet Report 2026 WWF summary

stories.ai_why: Major international biodiversity report tracking global wildlife population trends.

points: The WWF and ZSL released the Living Planet Report 2026 titled The Science of Hope, noting a 73% average decline in monitored wildlife populations between 1970 and 2022.
The decline is primarily driven by habitat loss, overexploitation, and climate change, which together account for roughly 67% of total biodiversity loss.
Freshwater ecosystems suffered the steepest collapse at 85%, followed by terrestrial ecosystems at 69% and marine ecosystems at 59%.
Latin America and the Caribbean recorded the steepest regional decline of 95%, followed by Africa at 80% and Asia-Pacific at 49%.
The report highlights that energy, food, and finance systems must reach positive tipping points before 2030 to meet the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework deadlines.

India demonstrates that biodiversity decline can be reversed through scientific conservation, community participation, and targeted financing, supported by successes in tigers, lions, and other species.

stories.title: Beyond the CJI: What independence should mean for Election Commission appointments
stories.summary: To select independent ECs, look beyond the CJI

explain.headline: Beyond the CJI: What Independence Should Mean for Election Commission Appointments
static: Article 324 of the Constitution provides for the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to be vested in an Election Commission.

Article 324(2) states that the Election Commission shall consist of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners, if any, as the President may from time to time fix.
Appointments of the CEC and ECs are made by the President, subject to the provisions of any law made in that behalf by Parliament.

Historically, before the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act of 2023, ECs were appointed directly by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers.

The Supreme Court in Anoop Baranwal v Union of India (2023) ruled that appointments should be made by the President on the advice of a committee comprising the PM, LoP, and the CJI, pending legislation by Parliament.
explain.what: The article examines the constitutional debate surrounding the appointment process of Election Commissioners under the 2023 Act, questioning whether executive dominance in the selection committee compromises institutional neutrality.
explain.why_in_news: The issue is in the news due to a split verdict by the Supreme Court in Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India, which challenges the 2023 Act and has referred the matter to a Constitution bench.
explain.background: Article 324 empowers the President to appoint Election Commissioners subject to parliamentary legislation, a legislative gap that existed for decades until the Supreme Court intervened in Anoop Baranwal and Parliament subsequently enacted the 2023 law.
significance: It addresses the foundational constitutional question of institutional autonomy for the Election Commission of India.
It evaluates the balance of power between the executive and the opposition in high-level statutory appointments.
It highlights the difference between judicial interim arrangements and durable parliamentary legislations.
prelims: The 2023 Act being challenged is the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Section 7 of the 2023 Act places the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and a Union Cabinet minister on the selection committee.
The Supreme Court case challenging the 2023 Act is Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India.
Earlier landmark judgments mentioned include Anoop Baranwal v Union of India and T N Seshan v Union of India.
explain.mains: Examine the constitutional debates surrounding the appointment mechanism of Election Commissioners. To what extent does institutional independence depend on selection arithmetic rather than tenure and removal safeguards? (15 Marks, 250 Words)
explain.who: Supreme Court, B R Ambedkar, Justice Dipankar Datta, Justice Satish Chandra Sharma
explain.video_query: Election Commission appointment Act 2023 Supreme Court debate

stories.ai_why: Examines appointment process and independence of Election Commissioners.

points: The Supreme Court split in Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India challenges Section 7 of the 2023 Act, which places the PM, LoP, and a Union Cabinet minister on the EC selection committee.
Justice Dipankar Datta noted the LoP could become ornamental, while Justice Satish Chandra Sharma referred the constitutional question to a larger bench.
The 2023 Act replaced the temporary selection committee setup by the Anoop Baranwal judgment, which included the CJI, the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition.
The Anoop Baranwal judgment did not hold that the CJI must permanently occupy the third seat or that Parliament could never give the government a numerical majority.
The core issue is whether the government's assured voting power in the selection committee is compatible with the neutrality expected of the election watchdog.
Past cases like T N Seshan v Union of India caution against equating a numerical majority within the Commission with executive capture, citing independent conduct by appointed members.
Indian laws use various appointment models, such as the Central Vigilance Commissioner and Chief Information Commissioner panels where two of three members belong to the government.
Conversely, the CBI Director is selected by a committee comprising the PM, LoP, and the CJI or a nominated Supreme Court judge.
The upcoming Constitution bench must formulate a durable principle to define the minimum non-government safeguard that Parliament must preserve under Article 324.

explain.headline: Apple Pay Launch in India Highlights RBI's Outcome-Based Regulation
static: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India's central banking institution established on April 1, 1935, under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, responsible for regulating the monetary policy and payment systems.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) is an umbrella organisation for operating retail payments and settlement systems in India, created by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) in India includes foundational identity (Aadhaar), fast payment rails (UPI), document wallets (DigiLocker), consent frameworks (Account Aggregator), and open commerce (ONDC).

Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) is a security process where a user provides two different authentication factors to verify themselves, widely mandated by RBI for digital transactions to prevent fraud.
explain.what: Apple Pay launched in India on September 30, enabled by RBI's new outcome-based regulatory framework that permits device-native biometrics instead of mandatory OTPs for card payments.
explain.why_in_news: Apple Pay arrived in India after the RBI issued its Authentication Mechanisms for Digital Payment Transactions Directions.
explain.background: RBI shifted from mandating specific authentication technologies like OTPs to regulating outcomes and principles, enabling flexible authentication methods like device biometrics.
significance: Demonstrates the effectiveness of outcome-based regulation in fostering technological innovation in digital payments.
Addresses security vulnerabilities associated with OTP-based fraud while reducing payment friction.
Highlights the need for accountability when global technology platforms integrate into India's digital security chain.
prelims: Apple Pay arrived in India on September 30.
NPCI introduced on-device biometric authentication as an alternative to the UPI PIN in October 2025.
UPI carries roughly 84% of India's digital payment volume.
RBI's Authentication Mechanisms for Digital Payment Transactions Directions were issued in September 2025.
explain.mains: Examine how outcome-based regulation by the RBI can foster technological innovation in digital payments while ensuring robust consumer protection and security accountability.
explain.who: Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Apple, National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)
explain.video_query: RBI outcome based regulation Apple Pay India UPI

stories.ai_why: Highlights RBI's outcome-based regulation framework enabling fintech innovations like Apple Pay.

points: Apple Pay arrived in India on September 30, twelve years after its global debut, enabling users to pay via iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches without an OTP.
The launch was made possible by a regulatory breakthrough rather than just a commercial one, moving away from mandating OTPs which had become targets for fraudsters.
The core issue is how regulation should adapt to new technologies like device-native biometrics while maintaining security, consumer protection, accountability, and interoperability.
RBI's Payments Vision 2025 contemplated alternatives such as behavioural biometrics, digital tokens, and risk-based checks, leading to outcome-based regulation instead of prescribing specific tools.
The Authentication Mechanisms for Digital Payment Transactions Directions of September 2025 retain two-factor authentication but widen the choice of factors, including device-native biometrics.
NPCI already introduced on-device biometric authentication for UPI in October 2025, and Apple Pay now extends this transition into card payments.
Apple Pay in India does not yet support RuPay or UPI, which carry about 84 percent of India's digital payment volume, serving as a beginning for credit card holders on global networks.
Moving authentication into devices makes manufacturers part of the security chain, requiring RBI and issuers to ensure platform partners are held to strict accountability standards.

explain.headline: RBI raises repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 percent
static: The Monetary Policy Committee is a statutory body established under Section 45ZB of the Reserve Bank of India Act of 1934.
It consists of six members: the RBI Governor as Chairperson, a Deputy Governor, an officer of the Bank, and three external members appointed by the central government.
The primary mandate of the MPC is to determine the policy interest rate required to achieve the inflation target set by the central government.
The Central Government, in consultation with the RBI, notifies the inflation target in the Official Gazette once every five years.
The target inflation rate is set at 4% with a tolerance band of +/- 2% (upper tolerance of 6% and lower tolerance of 2%).
If the RBI fails to meet the inflation target for three consecutive quarters, it must submit a report to the central government explaining the reasons and remedial actions.
explain.what: The RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% and shifted its policy stance to calibrated tightening to combat rising inflation.
explain.why_in_news: The move came in response to inflation staying above the 4% comfort level for three months and reaching 4.8% in August.
explain.background: The MPC uses interest rate tools to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of economic growth, backed by statutory powers under the RBI Act.
significance: Signals a shift away from monetary easing to protect the economy from persistent inflationary pressures.
Demonstrates the central bank's commitment to keeping inflation within the prescribed statutory limits.
Reflects confidence in the domestic economy's growth momentum, with real GDP growing at 7.8% in the first quarter of FY 2026-27.
prelims: The repo rate was increased by 25 basis points to 5.5%.
The Monetary Policy Committee voted 4-2 to shift its stance to calibrated tightening.
Consumer price inflation was 4.8% in August.
Real GDP grew at 7.8% in the first quarter of FY 2026-27.
explain.mains: Discuss the rationale behind the recent shift in the RBI's monetary policy stance towards calibrated tightening and examine its implications for economic growth and inflation management.

explain.video_query: RBI repo rate hike monetary policy stance explained

points: The Reserve Bank of India increased the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% in a unanimous call by the Monetary Policy Committee.
The MPC also delivered a 4-2 verdict shifting its monetary stance from neutral to calibrated tightening, indicating no near-term easing.
This latest hike is the first since February 2023, following cumulative cuts of 125 basis points in 2025 and a subsequent hold at 5.25%.
The hike was triggered by rising inflation, a decline in agricultural output due to a deficient southwest monsoon, and unfavorable geopolitics.
Inflation exceeded the 4% comfort level over the past three months, reaching 4.8% in August, with current financial year estimates rising to 5.2%.
Challenging geopolitical developments including the reescalation of the war in West Asia in September drove high crude and commodity prices.
RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra stated that future rate increases depend on growth-inflation dynamics, supported by a strong Q1 real GDP growth of 7.8%.
While housing loans may become dearer and discretionary spending face pressure, the robust economy allows absorption of the higher rate to curb inflation.

explain.headline: India’s criminal codes say nothing about facial recognition tools. 3 amendments can fix this
static: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) form the foundational criminal law framework in India, replacing older colonial-era codes.
Section 63 of the BSA regulates the admissibility of electronic records in court, requiring specific certificates and hash values to verify authenticity against tampering.
The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 empowers law enforcement agencies to collect physical and biological measurements, including photographs and iris scans, from detainees and convicts.
The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) is mandated under the Identification Act to process and store these biometric records and share them with law enforcement agencies.
explain.what: The article discusses the legal vacuum surrounding the use of facial recognition technology by Indian police forces, noting that the new criminal codes regulate physical evidence but ignore software-based investigative leads, and suggests three legislative amendments.
explain.why_in_news: The Delhi Police disclosed to the Supreme Court that facial recognition identified thousands of individuals with criminal records at Jantar Mantar protests, exposing discrepancies and a lack of statutory regulation for the tool.
explain.background: India's criminal justice framework lacks specific statutory provisions governing automated facial recognition technology, despite laws authorizing biometric data collection and electronic evidence certification.
significance: Highlights the growing friction between emerging artificial intelligence tools in law enforcement and individual civil liberties.
Demonstrates critical gaps in statutory procedures governing warrantless arrests and the transparency of algorithmic leads in criminal trials.
Provides actionable legal recommendations to balance effective policing with judicial accountability and transparency.
prelims: Section 105 and Section 176(3) of the BNSS require video recording of searches, seizures, and crime scene visits by forensic experts.
Section 63(4) of the BSA mandates a certificate with Part A and Part B (including hash values) for admissibility of electronic records.
The Criminal Procedure Identification Act, 2022 empowers the NCRB to process and share measurements of convicts and arrestees.
Section 35 of the BNSS allows police officers to arrest without a warrant on credible information or reasonable suspicion.
explain.mains: Examine the regulatory gaps in India's new criminal codes concerning the use of facial recognition and artificial intelligence tools by law enforcement. Discuss the legislative amendments needed to ensure accountability and protect civil liberties.
explain.who: Delhi Police, Supreme Court of India, National Crime Records Bureau
explain.video_query: facial recognition police India criminal codes legal gaps

stories.ai_why: Legal gaps regarding facial recognition tools in India's criminal codes.

points: The Delhi Police used facial recognition at the Jantar Mantar protests in July and told the Supreme Court in August that the system identified 2,873 people with criminal records.
A subsequent report found that 22 of those individuals were lodged in prison during the protests, highlighting a gap in legal regulation for such software.
India's new criminal codes focus on recording evidence gathering but omit regulations for the software that decides whom police should target.
The BNSS and BSA require strict documentation and certificates with hash values for electronic records, but these rules do not cover algorithmic or facial matching outputs.
The Criminal Procedure Identification Act allows taking measurements like photographs and iris scans, but does not explicitly mention facial recognition or set accuracy standards.
Section 35 of the BNSS permits warrantless arrests based on credible information, but the law fails to specify whether a facial recognition match qualifies as such.
Preventive arrest provisions under Section 170 and document disclosure rules under Section 230 also lack clarity regarding how software-generated investigative leads are handled.

The author proposes three amendments to the Identification Act, BNSS, and BSA to mandate logging, restrict sole reliance on algorithmic outputs, and require expert certification of biometric error rates.

static: Quantum computing uses the principles of quantum mechanics, such as superposition and entanglement, to process complex data using qubits instead of classical bits.

Post-Quantum Cryptography refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against classical and quantum computer attacks.

significance: Highlights the urgency of preemptive cybersecurity measures in safeguarding national and global financial systems.

points: Financial regulators and banks are preparing for future quantum computers that could defeat current encryption used in online banking and payments.
The primary concern is not an immediate hack, but the lengthy time required to overhaul the global financial system's security architecture.
The harvest now, decrypt later threat involves attackers stealing and storing encrypted data today to decrypt it once advanced technology arrives.
Conventional computers use bits as 0 or 1, while quantum computers use qubits and exploit quantum mechanical properties for specific complex calculations.
Shor's algorithm running on a powerful fault-tolerant quantum computer could efficiently attack public-key systems that rely on large number factoring.
Upgrading bank encryption is complex because financial institutions rely on numerous interconnected applications, databases, and third-party vendor systems.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology has finalised post-quantum cryptography standards and selected encryption algorithms like ML-KEM and HQC.
Experts estimate existing encryption could face quantum threats within five to ten years, driving financial institutions to build migration strategies today.
India's financial sector is beginning to plan for the quantum transition, with the government asking the BFSI sector to build resilience.

static: Article 16(4) of the Constitution empowers the State to make provisions for the reservation of appointments or posts in favor of any backward class of citizens not adequately represented in the services under the State.
The Supreme Court in the landmark Indra Sawhney case (1992) capped the total reservation limit at 50 percent, except in extraordinary circumstances.
The 50 percent ceiling rule was reiterated by the Supreme Court in later judgments, including the Maratha reservation case (Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister).

points: The Madhya Pradesh High Court ruled that Other Backward Classes are entitled to a 14 percent reservation in state public services and higher education.
The court declined to uphold the increase of reservation from 14 percent to 27 percent enacted via Ordinance No. 2/2019 and the Amendment Act, 2019.
The court stated that data from Higher Education and Public Services shows OBCs are adequately represented and part of the mainstream under Article 16(4).

It noted that no extraordinary conditions or emergent situations exist to justify exceeding the Supreme Court's 50 percent reservation ceiling set in the Indra Sawhney and Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil cases.
Appointments made under the 2019 Amendment Act up to September 29, 2022, exceeding the 14 percent quota and up to 27 percent, are protected from removal.
Candidates appointed in excess of 14 percent between March 2019 and September 29, 2022, will have their appointments adjusted in the next three recruitment drives.
Appointments made after September 29, 2022, must adhere to an 87 percent cap, with the remaining 13 percent filled from unreserved category candidates.

The reforms aim to shift towards trust-based enforcement by reducing coercive powers and lowering compliance burdens for businesses.
The core issue is balancing taxpayer rights and ease of doing business with strict action against fraud, fake invoices, and ITC misuse.
The prosecution threshold is proposed to be raised from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore, and general penalty is reduced to Rs 10,000.
Goods in inter-State movement can now be inspected or detained only by supplier or destination State officers with specific intelligence and authorization.
Registration is streamlined with 61 percent of taxpayers receiving automatic registration within three working days, and small e-commerce sellers can register in one State.
Refund acknowledgements are shortened to 10 days, with 90 percent of claims released within three working days of acknowledgement.
An optional annual-return scheme is proposed for B2C businesses with turnover up to Rs 5 crore, along with faceless assessment for Central GST.
Most of these changes are expected to be implemented from 1 April 2027 to improve predictability and business cash flows.

explain.headline: Supreme Court Criticises Misuse of 1987 Katiji Precedent on Condonation of Delay
static: The Limitation Act, 1963 prescribes time limits for filing suits, appeals, and applications to prevent indefinite litigation and secure legal certainty.
Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits condonation of delay if the appellant satisfies the court that sufficient cause existed for not filing in time.
The legal maxim 'vigilantibus non dormientibus jura subveniunt' stipulates that the law assists only those who are vigilant, not those who sleep over their rights.
The Securities Appellate Tribunal is a statutory body established under Section 15K of the SEBI Act, 1992 to hear appeals against SEBI orders.
Decisions of the Securities Appellate Tribunal can be appealed directly before the Supreme Court of India on questions of law under Section 15Z.
explain.what: The Supreme Court dismissed appeals by Karvy Stock Broking against SAT orders refusing condonation of delay. The court criticised the misuse of its 1987 Katiji ruling as a blanket excuse for delayed legal filings.
explain.why_in_news: A Supreme Court bench refused to excuse Karvy's delayed appeal against SEBI penalties, strongly deprecating routine condonation of delays under past precedents.
explain.background: The Limitation Act sets rigid timelines for appeals, with Section 5 granting courts discretionary power to excuse delays only upon demonstration of sufficient cause.
significance: Enforces procedural discipline and discourages indefinite delays in regulatory and commercial litigation.
Affirms equal application of limitation laws to private litigants, public bodies, and statutory regulators.
Reinforces the finality of tribunal orders when statutory deadlines are breached without valid justification.
prelims: Collector, Land Acquisition v. Katiji (1987) established a liberal approach towards condoning delays in favour of substantial justice.
SEBI imposed penalties of 13 crore rupees on Karvy and 8 crore rupees on Parthasarathy for diverting 1,442.95 crore rupees.
Appeals from the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) lie directly to the Supreme Court of India.
explain.mains: Strict adherence to statutory limitation periods is essential for commercial certainty and the rule of law. Discuss in light of recent judicial pronouncements on condonation of delay.
explain.where: Supreme Court of India, New Delhi
explain.who: Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu; Karvy Stock Broking Limited; C Parthasarathy; SEBI
explain.video_query: Supreme Court condonation of delay Katiji judgment Karvy SEBI

stories.ai_why: Supreme Court observations on judicial precedent and delay condonation.

points: The Supreme Court dismissed appeals by Karvy Stock Broking and its former chairman challenging SAT orders that rejected condonation of delay.
Appellants approached the apex court after the Securities Appellate Tribunal refused to condone delays in challenging financial penalties imposed by SEBI.
The core issue concerned whether courts should routinely adopt a liberal approach to condoning procedural delays under the doctrine of substantial justice.
Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu lamented the 1987 Katiji ruling, stating it has driven the nation back by becoming a routine excuse.
In the 1987 Katiji judgment, the apex court condoned a four-day delay while advocating that substantial justice should prevail over technical considerations.
The bench noted that regulatory authorities like SEBI and private litigants would face equal strictness regarding time-barred statutory appeals.
The dispute stemmed from SEBI penalising Karvy and C Parthasarathy for diverting approximately 1,442.95 crore rupees of client securities.
SEBI had imposed fines of 13 crore rupees on Karvy, 8 crore rupees on Parthasarathy, and banned both for seven years.
The dismissal leaves SAT orders undisturbed without examining the merits of SEBI findings, signalling strict enforcement of statutory limitation periods.

explain.headline: New CAPF Act Takes Effect, Reserving Top Posts for IPS Officers
static: Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) function under the authority of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, and are tasked with internal security, border guarding, and critical asset protection.

The Indian Police Service (IPS) is an All India Service under Article 312 of the Constitution, whose officers frequently occupy senior leadership positions in central and state law enforcement agencies.
Group-A General Duty officers in the CAPFs form the backbone of the officer cadre, responsible for tactical command and administrative management of battalions and formations.
Service matters, deputation quotas, and cadre reviews in paramilitary and police organisations have long been contentious issues involving administrative control and officer morale.
Supreme Court directions regarding cadre reviews aim to balance the organizational efficiency of security forces with equitable career progression opportunities for direct-entry cadre officers.

explain.background: The Act introduces a common umbrella framework for Group-A officers in five forces, reigniting a long-running dispute between direct-entry cadre officers and the government over IPS deputation quotas.
significance: It permanently alters the command structure and leadership pathways in India's premier internal security and border-guarding forces.
It highlights the friction between legislative policy implementation and judicial directions regarding cadre progression and officer morale.
It serves as a critical case study for civil services examinations on administrative governance, police reforms, and institutional litigations.
prelims: The CAPF (General Administration) Act came into force on October 8, 2026.
The Act applies to five forces: CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, and SSB.
Under the new law, 50% of Inspector General (IG) posts are filled through IPS deputation.
Special Director General (SDG) and Director General (DG) posts are filled exclusively through deputation.

points: The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026 came into force across the country on October 8, 2026, establishing a common legal framework for recruitment and service conditions.
The new law covers five major security forces: CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, and SSB, replacing divergent rules and addressing past service-related litigations.
The core dispute involves the reservation of senior command posts for Indian Police Service officers on deputation, which cadre officers argue will severely restrict their promotional opportunities.
Serving and retired CAPF officers have approached the Supreme Court with petitions and contempt proceedings challenging the validity and implications of the legislation.
The legal battle follows a May 2025 Supreme Court judgment and an October 2025 dismissal of a review petition, where the court had directed a progressive reduction of IPS deputation within two years.

The core debate centers on balancing the need for advanced manufacturing investments and global supply chain integration with national security safeguards.

explain.headline: UAPA Anti-Terror Law Demands Urgent Reform Amid Concerns Over Civil Liberties
static: The 16th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963 empowered Parliament to impose reasonable restrictions on Article 19 freedoms in the interest of India's sovereignty and integrity.
Enacted originally in 1967 to curb secessionist movements, UAPA was comprehensively amended in 2004, 2008, 2012, and 2019 to incorporate counter-terrorism provisions.
In NIA v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali (2019), the Supreme Court ruled that courts cannot examine the admissibility of prosecution evidence at the bail stage under Section 43D(5).
In Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb (2021), the Supreme Court affirmed that constitutional courts can grant bail for Article 21 violations despite statutory restrictions.
In Arup Bhuyan review (2023), the Supreme Court held that mere continued membership of an association declared unlawful is punishable under the UAPA.
explain.what: The procedural severity and strict bail conditions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act are facing renewed scrutiny for causing years of pre-trial detention without trial. Reform advocates demand statutory limits on detention, clearer legal definitions, and safeguards for civil liberties.

explain.background: The UAPA was enacted in 1967 to counter threats to national sovereignty and later modified into India's primary anti-terror legislation with stringent procedural deviations from ordinary criminal law.
significance: Highlights the constitutional friction between anti-terror provisions and fundamental rights like Article 21.
Examines the misuse of protracted pre-trial detention as de facto punishment due to restrictive bail clauses.
Focuses attention on the need for institutional accountability and statutory compensation for wrongful imprisonment.
prelims: Section 43D(5) of UAPA restricts bail if allegations are prima facie true based on prosecution reports.
Section 43D(2) permits police custody up to 30 days and charge-sheet filing time up to 180 days.
Section 35 of UAPA, amended in 2019, empowers the Centre to designate individuals as terrorists.
NCRB data shows conviction rates under the UAPA remain between 3 and 5 percent.
explain.mains: Anti-terror laws like UAPA, designed for national security, risk becoming tools of political repression. Evaluate the constitutional concerns and judicial responses in this context.

points: The second death anniversary of acquitted Delhi University Professor G.N. Saibaba renewed calls for comprehensive reform of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
The demand stems from concerns over prolonged pre-trial detention, vague offense definitions, and low conviction rates despite stringent procedural hurdles.
At stake is the constitutional balance between preserving national security and safeguarding fundamental rights, particularly the right to personal liberty under Article 21.
Section 43D(5) bars bail if the court finds allegations prima facie true, inverting the principle of bail as the standard rule.
Section 43D(2) expands police remand to 30 days and extends the pre-charge investigation period up to 180 days.
The 2019 amendment enabled the Central Government under Section 35 to designate individuals as terrorists without prior judicial conviction.
Official NCRB data indicates conviction rates under UAPA hover below 3 to 5 percent, resulting in years of incarceration before acquittal.
Proposed reforms include defining terrorist acts precisely, mandating time-bound trials, easing bail restrictions, and providing statutory compensation for wrongful incarceration.

points: The Reserve Bank of India announced stricter regulations for foreign exchange derivatives on October 10 to maintain orderly market functioning and shield the rupee.
The rules were introduced amid changing market conditions and a shrinking of India's forex reserves by $13 billion to $734.6 billion in four consecutive weekly declines.
Authorised dealers are now restricted from permitting customers to rebook rupee-linked foreign exchange derivative contracts cancelled after the issuance of directions.
The threshold for undertaking foreign exchange derivative transactions without establishing underlying exposure was slashed from $100 million to $5 million.
Permissible limits for exchange-traded currency derivatives involving the rupee without underlying exposure were also lowered to $5 million across all stock exchanges combined.
Authorised dealers must obtain customer undertakings confirming that underlying exposures have not been hedged elsewhere to prevent multiple hedging.
A new Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve requires dealers to keep a cash reserve with the RBI equal to 20% of the notional amount for transactions exceeding $2 million.
Banks must now maintain at least 99% of their prescribed daily Cash Reserve Ratio from October 16, up from 90% previously, reducing liquidity management flexibility.

stories.title: 2025 ruling ‘last nail in coffin’ of 1987 order on delay condonation: SC
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has hailed a 2025 judgment authored by Justice JB Pardiwala as the “last nail in the coffin” of its 1987 ruling that it said has been repeatedly invoked to secure condonation of delay, warning that an overly liberal approach to limitation has kept the country “driven back” for decades by allowing litigation to continue despite inordinate delays

video.query: Supreme Court strict limitation law delay condonation explained

explain.headline: Supreme Court terms 2025 ruling last nail in coffin of 1987 delay condonation order
static: The law of limitation prescribes the time-frame within which different types of legal suits, appeals, or applications must be filed in courts.

Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, allows courts to admit appeals or applications after the prescribed period if the appellant satisfies the court of sufficient cause for not preferring it within time.
The concept of sufficient cause is not strictly defined in the statute, leaving its interpretation to judicial discretion based on the facts and circumstances of each case.

While courts traditionally balanced technical rules of limitation with the delivery of substantial justice, recent judicial trends emphasize strict adherence to deadlines to prevent perpetual uncertainty.
explain.what: The Supreme Court praised a 2025 judgment for dismantling a lenient 1987 precedent on condoning judicial delays, signalling a strict enforcement of limitation periods for both private and public litigants.
explain.why_in_news: The observations were made while the Supreme Court dismissed appeals by Karvy Stock Broking Limited and its former chief against SAT orders refusing to condone delays.
explain.background: For decades, courts relied on a 1987 ruling to adopt a liberal approach to condoning legal delays in the name of substantial justice, a practice now heavily discouraged by the apex court.
significance: It curtails the misuse of condonation of delay applications by litigants seeking to revive stale claims.
It holds government bodies and regulators like SEBI to the same strict deadlines as private citizens, curbing bureaucratic delays.
It promotes judicial finality and protects successful litigants from prolonged and uncertain litigation.
prelims: The 1987 ruling criticized by the Supreme Court is Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag Vs Mst Katiji.
The 2025 judgment referred to as the last nail in the coffin was authored by Justice JB Pardiwala in the Shivamma case.
The case involved appeals by Karvy Stock Broking Limited and C Parthasarathy against the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
The 2023 ruling cited on scrutiny of condonation is Sheo Raj Singh vs Union of India, authored by Justice Dipankar Datta.
explain.mains: Examine the tension between the justice-oriented liberal approach to the law of limitation and the judicial insistence on timely litigation, particularly concerning state instrumentality actions.
explain.who: Justice Dipankar Datta, Justice Sheel Nagu, Justice JB Pardiwala, Karvy Stock Broking Limited, SEBI, Securities Appellate Tribunal
explain.video_query: Supreme Court strict limitation law delay condonation explained

stories.ai_why: Landmark Supreme Court ruling on judicial precedent and delay condonation.

points: The Supreme Court criticized its 1987 ruling in Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag Vs Mst Katiji, stating it had become a panacea for condoning delays.
A bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu remarked that a 2025 judgment authored by Justice JB Pardiwala serves as the last nail in the coffin of the 1987 order.
The core issue is that an overly liberal approach to limitation periods has allowed litigation to continue indefinitely despite inordinate delays and bureaucratic indifference.
The bench made these observations while dismissing appeals by Karvy Stock Broking Limited and its former chairman C Parthasarathy against orders of the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
SAT had refused to condone delays in challenging penalties imposed by the Securities and Exchange Board of India.
The 2025 Shivamma case judgment held that a litigant seeking condonation must explain the entire period from the commencement of limitation until actual filing.
The court also refused to extend special indulgence to government bodies or public instrumentalities for procedural red tape or bureaucratic delays.
The bench emphasized that the strict limitation standards will apply equally to both private litigants and regulatory bodies like SEBI.

static: Tribunals in India derive their constitutional basis from Articles 323A and 323B, which were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976.
Article 323A deals exclusively with administrative tribunals for public service matters, while Article 323B provides for tribunals on other matters like taxation and industrial disputes.
Parliament or State Legislatures can establish these tribunals by law to adjudicate disputes outside the normal hierarchical court system.

static: PM-WANI stands for Prime Minister’s Wi-Fi Access Network Interface, a flagship scheme approved by the Union Cabinet in December 2020 and launched by the Department of Telecommunications.
The architecture framework comprises Public Data Offices that fetch internet bandwidth, Public Data Office Aggregators that handle authorization and accounting, and App Providers that register users.
The scheme aims to bypass licensing fees for public Wi-Fi providers to proliferate broadband access, encourage local entrepreneurship, and boost ease of doing business.
BharatNet, originally called the National Optical Fibre Network, is the world's largest rural broadband project funded by the Universal Service Obligation Fund to connect all gram panchayats.

points: India has made major progress in digital payments and mobile data, but public Wi-Fi remains underdeveloped with only around four lakh hotspots compared to millions in countries like France.
The Department of Telecommunications launched the PM-WANI scheme to accelerate internet proliferation by setting up public Wi-Fi hotspots across the country.
Under PM-WANI, Public Data Offices establish and operate WANI-compliant Wi-Fi hotspots by partnering with Public Data Office Aggregators to deliver affordable internet services.
As of February 2026, data shows over four lakh operational public Wi-Fi hotspots, 207 aggregators, and 113 app providers registered under the framework.
Public Wi-Fi drives digital inclusion, lowers internet costs, generates local employment, improves rural connectivity, and reduces pressure on mobile data networks using unlicensed spectrum.
Implementation faces severe hurdles including high backhaul costs for small operators, resistance from incumbent telecom players, weak execution, and poor last-mile retail distribution.
The author proposes integrating BharatNet with PM-WANI, enforcing fair wholesale pricing, guaranteeing service quality, promoting alternative technologies, and fostering open networks.

Pending cases with the Central Information Commission rose significantly to 39,121 from 24,102 on June 30, 2025.
Tripura SIC would take an estimated 19 years and 8 months to clear a matter filed on July 1, 2026.

static: The Right to Information Act was enacted in 2005 to empower citizens, promote transparency and accountability, and give effect to the freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).

Sections 12 and 15 provide for the constitution of the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions respectively to handle appeals and complaints.

explain.headline: A Common Language for Justice and Linguistic Inclusion in Indian Courts
static: Article 348 of the Constitution deals with the language to be used in the Supreme Court and in High Courts and for Acts, Bills, etc., prescribing English unless Parliament provides otherwise.

Section 7 of the Official Languages Act, 1963, permits the use of Hindi or state official languages for High Court judgments, decrees, and orders with prior consent of the President and authoritative English translations.
The 216th Report of the Law Commission of India examined issues relating to judicial administration, language proficiency, and the global importance of English in legal education and practice.
SUVAS (Supreme Court Vidhik Anuvaad Software) is an artificial intelligence-assisted tool deployed by the judiciary to translate legal documents and judgments into various Indian regional languages.
The Bharatiya Bhasha Samiti plays a role in developing a common core vocabulary to facilitate the accurate translation of legal materials into Indian languages.
explain.what: The debate over judicial languages in India centers on whether to retain English as the primary language of higher courts or transition to regional languages to improve public access to justice.

explain.background: Article 348 mandates English for higher judiciary proceedings, but constitutional provisions and statutory acts permit regional languages in High Courts under specific conditions and Presidential consent.
significance: It addresses the gap between complex English-based legal proceedings and ordinary citizens with limited language proficiency.
It balances national judicial consistency, legal precedents, and administrative convenience with linguistic inclusiveness.
It highlights the role of modern AI tools like SUVAS in bridging the language divide in the Indian judicial system.

topics.n: Language policy and the three-language formula

points: The debate over making Hindi the official language of the Supreme Court highlights tensions between constitutional authority, judicial efficiency, and public access to justice.
Article 348(1)(a) prescribes English for proceedings in the Supreme Court and High Courts unless Parliament enacts a law otherwise.
The core issue is balancing the need for judicial consistency and a common legal framework with the linguistic barriers faced by non-English proficient citizens.

Under Article 348(2) and Section 7 of the Official Languages Act, 1963, certain states like Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Bihar authorized Hindi in their High Courts with the President's prior consent.
In 2012 and 2016, the Supreme Court's Full Court rejected proposals to introduce regional languages like Tamil, Gujarati, Hindi, Bengali, and Kannada in various High Courts.
Legal precedents like Madhu Limaye v. Ved Murti (1970) ruled that an intervener could not insist on arguing in Hindi if the Bench could not follow.
Replacing English with Hindi alone would ignore India's vast linguistic diversity, requiring a multi-language approach rather than a single-language replacement.
Technological initiatives like SUVAS (Supreme Court Vidhik Anuvaad Software) have translated tens of thousands of Supreme Court and High Court judgments into regional languages.

Future reforms require strengthening technological infrastructure, training legal personnel, standardizing legal vocabulary through the Bharatiya Bhasha Samiti, and following constitutional procedures.

explain.headline: GST Reforms Aim to Boost Compliance by Removing Fear, Widening Tax Base
static: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) is an indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services in India, replacing a slew of central and state indirect taxes.
The GST Council is a constitutional body established under Article 279A of the Constitution, chaired by the Union Finance Minister and comprising state finance ministers.
Input Tax Credit (ITC) allows businesses to claim credit for the GST paid on purchases used in the course of business, avoiding cascading tax effects.
An inverted duty structure occurs when the tax rate on inputs is higher than the rate on finished goods, leading to accumulation of unutilised ITC.
Faceless administration utilizes technology to eliminate physical interaction between taxpayers and tax officials, ensuring consistency, transparency, and accountability in tax proceedings.
explain.what: Recent GST reforms propose removing the power of arrest, shifting to a centralized faceless administration, and easing Input Tax Credit rules to foster a trust-based tax regime.

explain.background: Following rate rationalisation, recent GST Council decisions focus on lowering administrative friction, leveraging technology, and removing fear to widen the tax base.
significance: Reduces harassment and compliance burdens for genuine and small businesses.
Leverages technology and B2C e-invoicing to curb tax fraud while widening the formal tax base.
Streamlines multi-state tax administration through a centralized and faceless platform, improving ease of doing business.
prelims: Gross GST collection grew by 11.6% in H1 2026 and 15% in Q2 2026-27.
Reported B2C supply rose from Rs 45.91 lakh cr in 2022-23 to Rs 86.55 lakh cr in 2025-26.

The effective tax rate on domestic taxable supply fell from 11.74% to 10.84%.
explain.mains: Discuss how shifting from a deterrence-heavy tax architecture to a trust-based administration can enhance compliance and broaden the tax base under the GST regime.

points: The GST Council introduced major reforms aimed at boosting compliance by moving toward a trust-based tax administration and removing fear from the system.
The recent reforms were triggered by the success of rate rationalisation from the previous year, which led to a surge in gross GST collection and average monthly taxable supply.
The core issue being addressed is the cost of visibility for businesses, as fear of stringent measures like arrest kept small traders away from the tax base.
The GST Council recommended removing the power of arrest from GST law to encourage small traders to register and grow within the formal system.
To counter fraud without harming genuine taxpayers, enforcement will now focus on fewer cases, stronger evidence, faster trials, and better technology like invoice matching.
Sales to consumers (B2C) are a key focus area, with e-invoicing for B2C supplies expected to be ready for roll-out by April 2027 to prevent fake input tax credit generation.
The government announced the creation of a centralised, faceless platform for CGST administration to eliminate multiplicity of proceedings for multi-state businesses.
Other trust-based measures include automatic registration amendments, thresholds for notices, correction of return errors, faster refunds, and limits on vehicle interception.
Significant changes to Input Tax Credit (ITC) rules, including refunds on capital goods, are expected to free up working capital and encourage investment.
