explain.headline: UAPA Bail Bar for Foreigners Applies Only If Initial Entry Was Illegal: Supreme Court
static: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) is India's primary anti-terror law enacted in 1967 to prevent unlawful activities associations.
Section 43D of the UAPA introduces special provisions for bail, making it harder for accused persons to secure release if the court is of the opinion that the accusation is prima facie true.

Statutory default bail or compulsory bail is governed under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), granted when the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet within the stipulated timeframe.

The National Investigation Agency (NIA) was established under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, following the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks to investigate terror-related crimes across states without special state permission.
explain.what: The Supreme Court clarified that the UAPA Section 43D(7) statutory bail bar for foreign nationals applies only if their initial entry into India was unauthorised or illegal, not when a legal entry on a valid visa later becomes overstayed.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court delivered this judgment while dismissing the Union government's appeal against a Madras High Court order restoring bail to a Sri Lankan national accused in a UAPA case.
explain.background: Under the UAPA, stringent bail conditions apply to certain accused individuals, while statutory default bail under the CrPC protects suspects when chargesheets are delayed.
significance: Clarifies the precise legal threshold required to invoke the stringent bail bar against foreign nationals under the UAPA.
Protects statutory default bail rights under Section 167(2) of the CrPC from being overridden by subsequent allegations unless initial entry conditions are met.
Emphasizes the necessity for investigative agencies to produce concrete material proving initial illegal entry rather than relying on subsequent visa overstays.
prelims: Section 43D(7) of the UAPA places restrictions on the grant of bail to foreign nationals.
Mohamed Rifas was accused in an FIR registered on April 2, 2018, at Keelakarai police station in Tamil Nadu.
The NIA took over the case and registered a separate FIR in 2019 alleging the accused was a Sri Lankan national who entered India in 2009.
The Madras High Court set aside the special court's bail cancellation order on December 12, 2023.
explain.mains: Analyze the legal distinction between lawful initial entry followed by visa overstay versus illegal initial entry in invoking statutory bail restrictions under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
explain.who: Supreme Court bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi
explain.video_query: Supreme Court UAPA bail bar foreign nationals explanation

stories.ai_why: Supreme Court clarifies statutory bar on bail under UAPA regarding foreigners.

points: The Supreme Court held that the statutory bail bar under Section 43D(7) of the UAPA applies to foreigners only if their initial entry into India was illegal.
The bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi clarified that lawful entry on a valid visa whose stay later becomes unauthorised does not attract this restriction.
The court dismissed the Union government's appeal against a Madras High Court order that had restored bail to accused Mohamed Rifas.
Rifas, a Sri Lankan national, was accused in a 2018 FIR involving offences under the IPC, UAPA, and Arms Act, and was initially granted statutory default bail in July 2018.
The NIA took over the case in 2019 and registered a separate FIR alleging Rifas entered India in 2009, overstayed his visa, and illegally obtained Indian identity documents.
A special court cancelled his bail in 2022, but the Madras High Court restored it in December 2023, noting the delay and lack of proof for initial illegal entry.
The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court order, noting the Centre failed to produce material prima facie establishing initial unauthorised entry into India.
The apex court also noted that the overriding effect of Section 43D(7) does not extend to statutory default bail granted under Section 167(2) of the CrPC.

explain.headline: Centre Amends Census Rules to Include Private Sector Employees and Teachers
static: The Census of India is conducted under the provisions of the Census Act, 1948, which empowers the central government to notify and conduct a census.
Section 4(2) of the Census Act empowers state governments to appoint persons as census officers, stating that such appointed persons shall be bound to serve.
Section 4A of the Census Act requires local authorities when directed by the Centre to provide necessary staff for census operations.
Sections 6 and 7 of the Census Act permit seeking assistance from private establishments and managers to take census of persons within their premises.
Article 23(1) of the Indian Constitution prohibits forced labour, but Article 23(2) explicitly permits the State to impose compulsory public service for public purposes.
The Census is a massive administrative undertaking requiring millions of enumerators and supervisors, historically relying heavily on government school teachers and local body officials.
explain.what: The Centre amended the Census Rules, 1990, to explicitly include private school teachers and private establishment employees as eligible Census enumerators, sparking legal debates over compulsory civilian service.
explain.why_in_news: The amendment was issued following judicial setbacks in the Bombay and Punjab and Haryana High Courts which granted protection against requisitioning private school staff for Census duties.
explain.background: The Census Act, 1948 provides statutory backing for conducting the census and appointing census officers, but courts have restricted the blanket requisitioning of private employees under specific sections.
significance: Highlights the tension between administrative necessity for a massive workforce and statutory limits on compelling private citizens to perform public duties.
Tests the scope of Article 23(2) of the Constitution regarding compulsory public service versus fundamental rights and individual livelihoods.
Brings crucial judicial scrutiny to subordinate legislation exceeding the powers granted by parent statutes.

points: The Centre amended the Census Rules, 1990, to explicitly include private school teachers and employees of private establishments as eligible Census enumerators.
This amendment was triggered by judicial setbacks in the Bombay and Punjab and Haryana High Courts which questioned the legal basis for requisitioning private staff.
The core legal debate centers on whether subordinate rules can exceed the parent Census Act, 1948, and if the government can legally compel private individuals to serve.
The amended rules expressly name teachers of government, local authority, aided, and unaided private institutions, while retaining the broader category of 'any person'.
The Ministry of Home Affairs stated the amendment aims to remove ambiguity and ensure smooth conduct of the massive nationwide Census exercise.
Sections 6 and 7 of the Census Act allow seeking assistance from private establishments mainly for counting people within their premises, not general door-to-door enumeration.
Article 23(2) of the Constitution permits compulsory service for public purposes provided it is non-discriminatory, supporting mandatory civilian service like Census duties.
Past judicial precedents, such as the LIC Jalandhar case in 2010, ruled that requisitioning employees under Section 7 is beyond the scope of the Act.
With a Gujarat High Court LIC ruling pending before the Supreme Court, final legal clarity on deploying private employees for Census duties remains unsettled.

Indira Gandhi pushed the amendment through a self-extended Lok Sabha during the Emergency while opposition leaders were jailed.
Acting on the Swaran Singh Committee, the amendment shifted subjects like education, forests, and administration of justice into the Concurrent List.
It also inserted Entry 2A into the Union List, enabling armed forces deployment in states without request, and froze Lok Sabha seat allocation based on the 1971 Census.
Although the 44th Amendment removed Article 257A regarding armed forces, it left the transfer of education, forests, and court administration intact.
Subsequent centralisation continues through executive tools like UGC regulations mandating nominee inclusion for vice-chancellor selections and conditional PM-SHRI grants.
With the delimitation freeze ending after the upcoming census, southern states now face the threat of losing parliamentary representation.
The author proposes placing the Seventh Schedule changes before the Inter-State Council under Article 263 to consult states before redrawing the map.

points: The Draft National Steel Policy Vision 2047, released on October 10, envisages nearly tripling steelmaking capacity with coal-based blast-furnaces accounting for 55% of production.
This coal-dependent pathway could lock in about $1.5 trillion in additional coking coal imports over the lifetime of the new plants.
India currently imports 92% of its coking coal at dollar-denominated prices, with coking coal accounting for roughly 40% of the cost of producing a tonne of steel.
The policy projects annual steel demand to triple from 72 million tonnes today to 236 million tonnes by 2047, while domestic coking coal supply will only reach 23 million tonnes by 2030.
Heavy reliance on imported coal leaves steelmakers and downstream sectors like construction and infrastructure vulnerable to international price volatility and freight disruptions.
Green hydrogen made with domestic renewable energy can replace coking coal in ironmaking, offering fixed rupee pricing for 25 years and inflation-proofing production.
Research indicates that new hydrogen-based plants can produce steel more cheaply than new blast furnaces by 2030 even under conservative cost-increase assumptions.
Green steel faces lower carbon costs under Europe's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), creating a major export opportunity for Indian manufacturers.

The image, captured in 2024 by a Vantor satellite from 90 kilometres away, shows a winged vehicle with open payload bay doors and another spacecraft attached.
China's spaceplane is an uncrewed, reusable vehicle designed to travel into orbit and return to Earth by gliding towards a runway.
China launched its first experimental reusable spacecraft in September 2020, with subsequent missions lasting 276 days, nine months, and a fourth starting in February 2026.
The open payload bay and the attached spacecraft suggest the vehicle can deploy equipment, release smaller objects, or conduct proximity operations.
Rendezvous and proximity operations involve manoeuvring close to other spacecraft for civilian servicing or potential military interference.
Both China and the US, which operates the comparable X-37B vehicle, maintain secrecy, creating uncertainty over whether the missions are civilian or military.
The capabilities demonstrated by reusable spaceplanes have significant implications for the security and protection of space infrastructure.

static: The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015 and entering into force in 2016, legally binds parties to hold global average temperature increases to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
The Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change is an independent, international multidisciplinary research collaboration tracking the relationship between public health and climate change.

Extreme heat stress during physical activity elevates risks of dehydration, heatstroke, and exacerbates underlying cardiovascular and respiratory illnesses, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations like outdoor workers and the elderly.

Emphasizes the co-benefits of clean energy transitions in reducing air pollution mortality alongside climate mitigation.

points: The 10th indicator report of the Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change found that health risks from climate change accelerated in the decade from 2016 to 2025.

Global annual average heat-related deaths increased by nearly 36% in the decade since the Paris Agreement, with human-caused climate change responsible for over 70% of the 710,000 heat deaths in 2023.
The core issue is that climate action has failed to keep pace with accelerating health harms, prompting calls to formally recognise climate change as a global health emergency.

In India, people were exposed to over 2,600 hours per year between 2016 and 2025 where heat posed a moderate or higher risk of heat stress during outdoor physical activity, exceeding 1990s levels by over 200 hours.
Indians also lost an estimated 64 hours of sleep annually due to high night-time temperatures between 2021 and 2025, about three hours more per year than the 1986-2005 average.
The report notes that extreme drought affected nearly 52% of the world's land for at least a month in 2025, while very extreme rainfall reached 17.2% of global land annually in 2016-2025.
On the positive side, clean energy investment reached a record $2.1 trillion in 2025, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths annually across at least 77 countries due to reduced air pollution.
The report was led by University College London in collaboration with the World Health Organization, tracking 54 indicators ahead of the COP31 UN climate conference.

explain.headline: High Court Acting Under Section 11 Cannot Extend Arbitrator's Mandate Under Section 29A
static: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is the principal law governing arbitration in India, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law.
Section 11 of the Act provides for the appointment of arbitrators by the Supreme Court or the respective High Court.
Section 29A prescribes time limits for making arbitral awards, mandating conclusion within twelve months from the completion of pleadings.
Section 2(1)(e) defines 'Court' as the principal civil court of original jurisdiction in a district, including the High Court exercising its ordinary original civil jurisdiction.
Amendments to the Arbitration Act over the years have aimed to minimize judicial intervention and expedite institutional and ad-hoc arbitrations in India.

explain.background: Section 11 deals with arbitrator appointments, while Section 29A governs time limits for arbitral awards and requires a specific designated 'Court' for extensions.
significance: Prevents jurisdictional overreach by High Courts when dealing with routine administrative appointments versus supervisory extensions.
Enhances procedural predictability in Indian arbitration law by strictly adhering to statutory definitions of the competent court.
Reduces delays caused by filing extension applications in incorrect judicial forums.
prelims: Core holding: Section 11 appointing courts lack suo motu or incidental power to extend mandates under Section 29A.

points: The Inter-State Council is a mechanism conceived to promote cooperative federalism in India, but it has largely remained dormant due to infrequent meetings and operational limitations.

Zonal Councils are statutory bodies established under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 to handle regional issues.
There are five Zonal Councils covering the North, South, East, West, and Central regions, chaired by the Union Home Minister.
The North Eastern Council was created under the North Eastern Council Act of 1972 to address unique regional development challenges.
The Inter-State Council serves to promote cooperative federalism, provide structured dialogue, build consensus, and investigate inter-State disputes under Article 263.
Key limitations of the Inter-State Council include infrequent meetings, its purely advisory nature, and the Centre's dominance in agenda setting.

explain.headline: What Is Logical Discrepancy In SIR And Why Supreme Court Is Testing Its Legality
static: The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional body established under Article 324 of the Constitution to superintend and conduct elections.
Special Intensive Revision is an administrative process undertaken by the ECI to verify and update electoral rolls by collecting enumeration forms and checking details.
Form 6 is used for fresh electoral enrolment, whereas Form 8 allows existing electors to report a change of residence or correct entries.
Electoral rolls form the foundational basis of democratic representation in India, ensuring that only eligible citizens exercise their franchise.
explain.what: The Supreme Court is examining the legality and procedural fairness of the ECI's 'logical discrepancy' checks used during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court raised questions during the Delhi SIR hearing, clarifying that its earlier interim permissions did not constitute a final ruling on the mechanism.
explain.background: The ECI conducts periodic revisions of electoral rolls to remove ineligible entries and ensure accurate voter lists, which has recently faced judicial scrutiny regarding transparency and procedural burdens on voters.
significance: It addresses the fundamental tension between maintaining electoral roll integrity and protecting citizens' constitutional right to vote.
It questions the extent of automation and lack of human scrutiny in flagging registered voters for verification.
It highlights procedural challenges faced by millions of voters, such as unmapped records and mechanical notices.
prelims: Around 19.34 lakh electors were categorised under logical discrepancies in the Delhi SIR exercise.
Approximately 33 lakh electors had details that could not be mapped to earlier electoral rolls.
Logical discrepancy checks involve details like voter age, parents' ages, family relationships, names, and gender particulars.
The Supreme Court bench handling the hearing comprised CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V Mohana.
explain.mains: Examine the constitutional and procedural concerns surrounding the use of automated data-matching and logical discrepancy checks in electoral roll revisions.
explain.who: Supreme Court, Election Commission of India
explain.video_query: Logical discrepancy in SIR Supreme Court Election Commission

stories.ai_why: Supreme Court examines constitutional validity of electoral/administrative discrepancy rules.

points: The Supreme Court clarified that the Election Commission of India's use of logical discrepancy checks during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls is not legally settled.
A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V Mohana questioned how electoral entries can be reopened based on patterns from revision exercises.
The core issue is whether automated or rule-based checks put existing voters at risk without adequate individual human scrutiny or transparent criteria.
During the Delhi SIR exercise, petitioners noted that approximately 19.34 lakh electors were categorized under logical discrepancies and 33 lakh were unmapped.
Logical discrepancies involve flagged entries where voter details like age, parents' ages, family relationships, names, or gender appear inconsistent.
The court questioned whether the ECI issued notices mechanically and stressed that a mismatch does not automatically prove ineligibility or fraud.
The bench asked the ECI to proactively reach out to missing electors rather than burdening registered voters who missed enumeration forms.
The Supreme Court is yet to deliver a final ruling, which will impact how the ECI conducts future electoral revisions using historical data-matching.

points: The Supreme Court struck down the Karnataka Civil Services (Validation of Selection and Appointment of 2011 Batch Gazetted Probationers) Act, 2022 as unconstitutional.

The core issue involved the legislature attempting to validate appointments made through a 2011 recruitment process marred by widespread corruption and nepotism.
The 2011 notification aimed to fill 362 posts, for which 1,38,307 candidates applied and 1,090 were eventually called for interviews.
A CID investigation revealed serious manipulation, including call records linking candidates with KPSC members, identical interview marks, and evidence destruction.
The Karnataka government previously cancelled the selection, and this cancellation was upheld earlier by both the Karnataka High Court and the Supreme Court.

static: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) is India's primary anti-terror legislation enacted in 1967 to prevent unlawful activities associations.
Section 43D of the UAPA modifies the general provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) regarding arrest, default bail, and police custody to deal stringently with terrorist offenses.
Default bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC is an indefeasible statutory right of an accused when the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet within the stipulated 60 or 90 days.
The National Investigation Agency (NIA) is the central counter-terrorism law enforcement agency of India, created via the National Investigation Agency Act of 2008 following the 2008 Mumbai attacks.
explain.what: The Supreme Court ruled that foreign nationality alone does not trigger the bail bars under Section 43D(7) of the UAPA unless the accused entered India illegally.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court delivered this judgment while dismissing the Union government's appeal against the Madras High Court's order restoring bail to Mohamed Rifas.
explain.background: Section 43D(7) of the UAPA restricts bail for foreign nationals who enter India illegally, but the Supreme Court clarified this does not invalidate statutory default bail earned due to delayed chargesheets.
significance: Protects the statutory right to default bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC even in stringent anti-terror laws like the UAPA.
Clarifies the precise legal threshold required under Section 43D(7), ensuring foreign nationality without illegal entry does not automatically deny personal liberty.
Reiterates strict judicial standards for cancelling granted bail based on subsequent chargesheets or misconduct.
prelims: Section 43D(7) of the UAPA restricts bail for foreign nationals entering India without authorization.
Default bail is granted under Section 167(2) of the CrPC when chargesheets are not filed on time.
The NIA took over the investigation into Mohamed Rifas in January 2019.
explain.mains: Examine the judicial interpretation of bail restrictions under Section 43D of the UAPA vis-a-vis the statutory right to default bail. How does the Supreme Court balance national security concerns with personal liberty?

explain.video_query: Supreme Court UAPA bail foreign national judgment explained

stories.ai_why: Supreme Court ruling on UAPA and bail rights for foreign nationals.

points: The Supreme Court held that an accused person's foreign nationality alone does not bar the grant of bail under the UAPA.
The bench clarified that the bail restriction under Section 43D(7) of UAPA applies only if the foreign national entered India illegally or without authorization.
The Court emphasized that a lawful initial entry into India does not become unauthorized simply because the stay subsequently becomes illegal or authorization is revoked.
The case involved Mohamed Rifas, a Sri Lankan national accused in a 2018 FIR regarding a conspiracy to disrupt communal harmony and commit terrorist acts.
Rifas had secured statutory default bail in July 2018 because the prosecution failed to file a chargesheet within the prescribed time under Section 167(2) of the CrPC.
The NIA later took over the case in January 2019, filed a chargesheet in January 2021, and a special court cancelled his bail in April 2022 under Section 43D(7).
The Madras High Court set aside the cancellation in December 2023, and the Supreme Court dismissed the Union government's appeal against this relief.
The Supreme Court ruled that Section 43D(7) does not override statutory default bail provisions and that bail cancellation requires sound, strong grounds rather than just subsequent chargesheets.

explain.headline: A richer measure of poverty: Why income alone is misleading
static: The Multidimensional Poverty Index is an international measure of acute multidimensional poverty covering over 100 developing countries.
It was first developed in 2010 by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the United Nations Development Programme.
The global MPI uses indicators across three dimensions: health, education, and standard of living, utilizing micro data from household surveys.
NITI Aayog acts as the nodal agency for the National Multidimensional Poverty Index in India, utilizing 12 indicators adapted to the national context.
explain.what: The article explains why income-based poverty measures are misleading and advocates for the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) as a more accurate metric of human wellbeing and deprivation.
explain.why_in_news: The discussion is prompted by recent global and national poverty estimates and data releases highlighting the divergence between income poverty and multidimensional poverty.
explain.background: Income-only measures fail to capture deprivations in health, education, and living standards, whereas the Multidimensional Poverty Index scores households across 10 indicators to reflect true living conditions.
significance: Highlights the limitations of GDP and income-based metrics in capturing true human wellbeing.
Shows how targeted public interventions in health, sanitation, and education can lower poverty independently of income growth.
Provides vital insights for Indian policy planning toward achieving inclusive development goals like Viksit Bharat.
prelims: The global MPI uses 10 indicators across health, education, and living standards.
About 5% of Indians lived below the $3 a day income line while 16.4% were multidimensionally poor according to the 2026 global MPI.
Bihar witnessed the largest headcount decline of about 18 percentage points from 52% to 34% between 2015-16 and 2019-21.
NITI Aayog’s national measure uses 12 indicators unlike the global MPI.
explain.mains: Critically examine the limitations of income-based poverty measures and discuss how the Multidimensional Poverty Index provides a more comprehensive framework for policy intervention in India.
keywords: Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative
explain.who: Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative, United Nations Development Programme, NITI Aayog
explain.video_query: Multidimensional Poverty Index India explained

stories.ai_why: Multidimensional poverty vs income-based measures is key economic syllabus topic.

points: Income-based poverty measures miss real life deprivations like poor nutrition, lack of clean cooking fuel, and bad housing.
The Multidimensional Poverty Index developed by OPHI and UNDP looks at 10 indicators across health, education, and living standards.
Each health and education indicator is worth three points, and each of the six living-standard indicators is worth one point.
A household scoring six points or more is counted as multidimensionally poor, with deprivations acting like a scorecard.
Income poverty and MPI can diverge significantly; about 5% of Indians live below $3 a day, but 16.4% are multidimensionally poor.
MPI is more amenable to direct government interventions such as providing toilets, electricity connections, and nutrition programmes.
Economic growth helps reduce poverty, but state-level GDP growth shows a weak correlation with reductions in state-level MPI.
Poorest states like Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh achieved the greatest reductions in multidimensional poverty between 2015-16 and 2019-21.
Nutrition remains a critical unfinished agenda as underweight rates have barely changed, pointing to the need for targeted policies.

Poverty, hunger, nutrition and food security

explain.headline: India's ESOP Tax Rules Need Reform to Ease Employee Burden
static: Employee Stock Option Plans (ESOPs) give employees the right to purchase company shares at a pre-determined exercise price after a vesting period.
Under current Indian income tax laws, the difference between the fair market value on the exercise date and the exercise price is taxed as perquisites.
Startups recognized by the Inter-Ministerial Board (IMB) currently enjoy deferred ESOP taxation up to five years or until sale/leaving the company.
Capital gains from the subsequent sale of shares are classified as short-term or long-term capital gains depending on the holding period from the date of exercise.

explain.background: ESOPs are taxed as perquisites at exercise based on the spread between fair market value and exercise price, creating a major cash outflow without matching cash inflows.
significance: Forces employees to prematurely sell equity incentives to cover tax liabilities.

Impairs India's vision of fostering deeper capital markets and a competitive corporate ecosystem.
prelims: Tax rate on perquisites for employees in the highest tax bracket can reach up to 39%.

points: India taxes Employee Stock Option Plans (ESOPs) at exercise by treating unrealised equity gains as perquisite salary income at rates up to 39%.
This creates a heavy cash flow burden because employees face massive tax bills on paper gains without receiving any actual cash.
The problem is severe in unlisted companies where share values rely on formulas rather than real market prices, locking up wealth for years.
Even in listed companies, employees must sell up to 40% of their shares immediately to pay taxes, disrupting their long-term investment goals.
Subsequent capital losses from ESOP sales cannot be set off against high salary income tax, leaving employees with asymmetric tax liabilities.
International jurisdictions like the US, Britain, and Singapore provide favorable tax treatments, deferrals, or separate regimes for employee equity.
The author proposes three reform approaches for India: deferring perquisite tax to liquidity events, taxing strictly at sale as capital gains, or taxing exercise spread at concessional rates.
Reforming ESOP taxation is about adjusting tax timing rather than granting exemptions, ensuring a culture of genuine employee ownership and deeper capital markets.

static: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is India's independent regional navigation satellite system developed by ISRO.

The primary service area covers the Indian landmass and an area extending up to 1,500 km beyond its boundaries.
The first-generation constellation consisted of IRNSS series satellites launched between 2013 and 2018.
The second-generation NVS satellites feature upgraded capabilities, including indigenous rubidium atomic clocks and the L1 civil navigation frequency band.
ISRO was established in 1969 and functions under the Department of Space, Government of India, headquartered in Bengaluru.

Scammers pose as law enforcement agents from agencies like the CBI, Narcotics Department, or RBI and use video conferencing to keep victims under constant visual surveillance.
Rapid digitalization without matching legal awareness, fear of law enforcement, sophisticated social engineering, and the easy availability of digital tools like mule accounts drive these crimes.

explain.headline: A virus found in cattle has infected a human. What makes zoonotic diseases dangerous?
static: Zoonotic diseases are infectious diseases that jump from non-human animals to humans, caused by various pathogens including viruses, bacteria, parasites, and fungi.
Pathogens must overcome biological barriers to infect humans, which can happen through direct contact, vector-borne transmission via insects, or contaminated food and water.
The Orthobunyavirus genus and Simbu serogroup comprise vector-borne viruses predominantly affecting ruminants and livestock across various global regions.
Vector control and animal health surveillance play critical roles in preventing potential zoonotic spillovers and safeguarding public health.
explain.what: French authorities confirmed the first-ever human infection of the livestock pathogen Shamonda virus in an immunocompromised patient who later died, highlighting the process of zoonotic spillover.
explain.why_in_news: The confirmation of the first recorded human case of the Shamonda virus in France on October 9 put the focus on zoonotic diseases.
explain.background: Shamonda virus is a livestock pathogen belonging to the Orthobunyavirus genus and Simbu serogroup, primarily spread by biting midges among animals like cattle, sheep, and goats.
significance: Highlights the ongoing risk of zoonotic spillover from livestock and animals to humans, especially in vulnerable individuals.
Emphasizes the necessity of robust animal disease surveillance and vector monitoring to detect emerging pathogens early.
Demonstrates how pathogens can cross species barriers even when human-to-human transmission is absent.
prelims: Shamonda virus belongs to the Orthobunyavirus genus and the Simbu serogroup.
The virus was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in 1965.
Shamonda virus is mainly transmitted through the bites of Culicoides midges.
The first documented human infection was reported in France in October 2026.
explain.mains: What is zoonotic spillover, and what factors determine whether an animal-borne infection becomes a wider public health concern? Discuss with examples.

explain.video_query: Shamonda virus human infection zoonotic spillover explained

stories.ai_why: Explainer on zoonotic diseases and spillover risks to humans.

points: French authorities confirmed the first recorded human infection of the Shamonda virus in a severely immunocompromised patient who later died.
The discovery highlights zoonotic spillover, where a pathogen moves from animals to humans, causing potential health risks when infecting a new host.
The Shamonda virus case is unusual because it was previously known only as a livestock pathogen without any documented human infections.
Authorities have stressed that there is currently no evidence of human-to-human transmission or a wider public health risk from this case.
Shamonda virus belongs to the Orthobunyavirus genus and Simbu serogroup, primarily affecting animals and transmitted mainly through Culicoides midge bites.
The virus was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in 1965 and has since been detected in animals across parts of Africa and Asia.
In livestock, the virus causes fever, diarrhoea, weakness, reduced milk production, and reproductive problems.
Transmission of animal diseases to humans can occur through direct contact, contaminated food, insect bites, or environmental exposure.
Public health authorities note that monitoring livestock, disease-carrying insects, and early reporting of unusual symptoms help identify emerging pathogens.

The core issue involves the severe downstream threat posed by flash floods and debris surges travelling through transboundary river systems.

Shintaphu Lake is among Bhutan's 17 glacial lakes identified as potentially dangerous, though its monitoring station did not trigger an alert.

static: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established on April 1, 1935, in accordance with the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were established under the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976, with the objective of providing credit and other facilities to small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, and rural artisans.
Priority Sector Lending (PSL) requires banks to allocate a specified portion of their bank lending to sectors economically vital but vulnerable, such as agriculture, MSMEs, and weaker sections.
Development Financial Institutions (DFIs) provide long-term finance for capital-intensive sectors like infrastructure, manufacturing, and large projects where commercial banks are hesitant to lend.

points: The Government of India has constituted the High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat to review the banking sector and recommend comprehensive reforms.
The committee was set up following an announcement made by Union Finance and Corporate Affairs Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in the Union Budget 2026-27 speech.
The core issue is whether India's current banking architecture is adequately equipped to meet the long-term financing and development requirements of a developed economy by 2047.
Former Central Vigilance Commissioner Suresh N. Patel has been appointed as the Chairman of the committee.
The members include RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu, former Indian Bank MD and CEO Padmaja Chunduru, and former RBI Deputy Governor N. S. Vishwanathan.
The Joint Secretary for Banking in the Department of Financial Services will serve as the Member Secretary of the committee.
The committee has been given a tenure of six months to formulate recommendations covering structural, institutional, regulatory, and legislative reforms.
The panel's mandate covers commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks, Cooperative Banks, Development Financial Institutions, and Non-Banking Financial Companies.
Key areas of review include global competitiveness, long-term capital requirements, AI adoption, cybersecurity, Priority Sector Lending, and financial inclusion.

explain.headline: ISRO Successfully Launches NVS-03 Navigation Satellite Using GSLV-F18
static: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is India's regional satellite navigation system, formerly known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS).
It is designed to provide accurate position information service to users in India and the region extending up to 1,500 km from its boundaries.
The space segment comprises a constellation of satellites operating in geosynchronous and geostationary orbits, supported by ground stations.
Atomic clocks on board navigation satellites are critical for maintaining ultra-precise timing to compute exact geographic locations on earth.
The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is a three-stage launch vehicle developed by ISRO, utilizing indigenous cryogenic upper stage technology in its Mk II and Mk III variants.
explain.what: ISRO launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket from Sriharikota to strengthen India's indigenous NavIC constellation.
explain.why_in_news: ISRO successfully placed NVS-03 into orbit at 11:51 pm on Friday to augment India's regional navigation network and reduce reliance on foreign systems.
explain.background: NavIC was conceived following the 1999 Kargil conflict to provide sovereign positioning and timing capabilities, though past missions faced setbacks due to imported atomic clock failures.
significance: Crucial for India's strategic autonomy and military operations by ensuring independent positioning, navigation, and timing services.
Reduces technological vulnerability by testing and incorporating indigenous atomic clock technology in space assets.
Expands civilian usability across smartphones, transport, aviation, and maritime sectors through new signal capabilities.
prelims: NVS-03 is the third satellite in India's second-generation Navigation Satellite series.
The satellite was launched using ISRO's GSLV-F18 vehicle from Sriharikota.
NVS-03 carries both an indigenous atomic clock and procured clocks.
The satellite is alternatively designated as IRNSS-1L.

The launch aims to plug critical gaps in India's strategic infrastructure and strengthen the indigenous NavIC constellation.
NVS-03 is the third satellite in the second-generation Navigation Satellite series and the twelfth overall under IRNSS.
The satellite carries an indigenous atomic clock along with procured ones to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers.
NavIC provides Standard Positioning Service for civilians and Restricted Service for strategic users across India and up to 1,500 km beyond.
The launch vehicle GSLV Mk II, once nicknamed the naughty boy, accurately placed the satellite into the intended elliptical orbit.
Future missions like NVS-04 and NVS-05 are expected soon to achieve a fully operational seven-satellite architecture.
The mission supports India's strategic push towards self-reliance, technological independence, and the goal of One Nation One Time.

static: Article 44 of the Indian Constitution, enshrined in the Directive Principles of State Policy, states that the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.
Personal laws relating to marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption have traditionally been governed by distinct religious codes rooted in Hindu, Muslim, Christian, and Parsi personal laws.
The Supreme Court of India has repeatedly emphasized the enactment of a Uniform Civil Code in landmark judgments, starting notably from the Shah Bano case in 1985.
Uttarakhand was the first state in independent India to pass a state-level Uniform Civil Code legislation in early 2024.
A Uniform Civil Code aims to replace these personal religious laws with a common set of governing rules applicable to all citizens regardless of their religious affiliation.

Addresses sensitive social issues such as polygamy and mandatory live-in relationship registration.

points: The Assam government has established an eight-member committee to frame rules for implementing the Uniform Civil Code Bill in the state.
The panel, headed by Home and Political Department Secretary Deba Prasad Misra, has been directed to submit draft rules within one month.
Assam passed The Uniform Civil Code, Assam, 2026 Bill on May 27 to establish a common legal framework for marriage, divorce, succession, and live-in relationships.
The Bill has been sent to the central government to secure the President's assent, as per an order issued by Additional Chief Secretary Ajay Tewari.
The legislation seeks to ban polygamy with up to seven years of imprisonment and make the registration of live-in relationships compulsory under threat of three months in jail.
The legislation exempts persons belonging to the Scheduled Tribes category and residing in Assam from its purview.
Assam became the third state in India, following Uttarakhand and Gujarat, to pass a Uniform Civil Code Bill.

explain.headline: Bombay High Court Halts Goa Tribal Population Notification Linked to Assembly Reservation
static: Article 332 of the Constitution provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in state Legislative Assemblies.
The 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001, froze the readjustment of electoral constituencies and reserved seat quotas until the first Census taken after 2026.
Constituency delimitation and allocation of seats are traditionally based on the latest published Census figures to reflect accurate demographic proportions.
Delimitation Commissions are statutory bodies constituted under Delimitation Acts, and their orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court.
explain.what: The Bombay High Court has restrained the Census Commissioner of India from notifying Goa's estimated Scheduled Tribe population. This notification is necessary for granting political reservation to Scheduled Tribes in the Goa Legislative Assembly.
explain.why_in_news: The Goa Bench of the Bombay High Court issued an interim stay on the notification while hearing a challenge against the 2025 Act on ST representation in Goa.
explain.background: Constitutional provisions mandate legislative seat reservations for Scheduled Tribes based on population proportions, but the nationwide delimitation freeze restricts changes until the first Census after 2026.
significance: Delays the proposed delimitation and legislative seat reservation for Scheduled Tribes ahead of Goa's expected 2027 Assembly polls.
Tests the constitutional limits of enacting special legislation to readjust legislative seats prior to the post-2026 Census.
Scrutinises administrative methods of estimating community populations without fresh Census enumerations.
prelims: The challenged law is the Readjustment of Representation of Scheduled Tribes in Assembly Constituencies of the State of Goa Act, 2025.
Section 3(1) of the Act empowers the Census Commissioner to estimate and notify Goa's ST population share.
The Census Commissioner presumed Goa's ST population share remained unchanged at 9.9 per cent based on the 2001 Census.
explain.mains: Discuss the constitutional safeguards for Scheduled Tribes' political representation in State Legislative Assemblies and evaluate the legal challenges surrounding constituency delimitation prior to the post-2026 Census.
explain.who: Census Commissioner of India, Goa Bench of Bombay High Court, Chief Minister Pramod Sawant, petitioner Edwin Lucio Fernandes
explain.video_query: Goa tribal reservation Bombay High Court order

stories.ai_why: Relevant for tribal rights, reservation policies, and judicial intervention under Schedule Tribes.

points: The Bombay High Court restrained the Census Commissioner from notifying Goa's estimated Scheduled Tribe population.
The order came on a petition by Edwin Lucio Fernandes challenging the constitutionality of a 2025 parliamentary Act.
At issue is whether the law impermissibly allows readjusting reserved seats before the first Census post-2026 is published.
The petitioner specifically contested Section 3(1) of the Act, which lets the Census Commissioner estimate and notify the ST population.
Counsel argued that once published, the population notification would become final and immune to court challenges.
Justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit S Jamsandekar noted the Census Commissioner had attempted estimation using 2001 or 2011 Census data.
The court observed that despite admitting data was inadequate, the Commissioner presumed Goa's ST share stayed unchanged at 9.9 percent.
Goa's Chief Minister said the state will urge the Centre to approach the Supreme Court to safeguard ST interests.

Natural gas migration refers to the movement of hydrocarbons through permeable subsurface strata from one lease block to an adjoining block operated by a different entity.

The mediator has been requested to take assistance of two domain experts as suggested by the parties involved in the dispute.

significance: It clarifies the interpretation of conflicting UGC regulations concerning teaching experience and research periods.
It sets a judicial precedent regarding the eligibility criteria for academic appointments in Indian universities.

points: The Supreme Court reserved its verdict on the appointment of Priya Varghese as an Associate Professor in the Malayalam Department at Kannur University.
The apex court stated that the appointment will be upheld if she proves she possesses the required eight years of teaching experience, and set aside if she fails.
The core legal dispute centers on whether the research period during a PhD can be counted as teaching experience under UGC regulations.
There is no dispute that Priya served as a teacher for four years, with the remaining four years under contention.
Priya's counsel argued that her research period as an Assistant Professor and her deputation as NSS director fulfill the eight-year experience criteria under UGC Regulation 4.1.
The UGC and the petitioner's counsel argued under Regulation 3.11 that research conducted as part of a PhD cannot be counted as work experience.
The Supreme Court orally disagreed with the UGC stance, observing that research carried out by an Assistant Professor as part of a PhD can count as teaching experience.
The court directed Priya Varghese's counsel to submit written details demonstrating the eight-year qualification to opposing lawyers.
The Supreme Court rejected the UGC request that the verdict should not be applied to other cases, stating clarity is required due to conflicting provisions.

explain.headline: Kerala High Court Seeks State Response on RTI Exemption for Vigilance Sections
static: The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 empowers Indian citizens to seek information from public authorities, promoting transparency and accountability.
Section 24 of the RTI Act exempts certain intelligence and security organisations specified by the Central and State Governments from the purview of the Act.
The first proviso to Section 24 explicitly mandates that information pertaining to allegations of corruption and human rights violations shall not be excluded even for listed exempt organisations.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) allows any public-spirited citizen or group to approach the High Court or Supreme Court for the protection of public interest.
Witness protection schemes provide for threat analysis, security measures, identity protection, and the establishment of dedicated witness protection cells and funds.

explain.background: State governments can exempt intelligence and security agencies under Section 24(4) of the RTI Act, subject to provisos protecting corruption and human rights disclosures.
significance: Tests the legal limits of executive power in exempting anti-corruption units from transparency laws.
Highlights the ongoing debate between administrative confidentiality and citizen rights to information on public corruption.
Stresses the importance of effective witness protection schemes in anti-corruption and criminal justice administration.
prelims: Section 24(4) of the RTI Act allows state governments to exempt specified intelligence and security organisations.
T1 and T2 sections belong to the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) in Kerala.
The Government Order exempting the sections was published in the Kerala Gazette on October 22, 2026.
The next hearing for the PILs is scheduled for November 18, 2026.
explain.mains: Examine the scope and limitations of exemptions granted to investigative and anti-corruption bodies under Section 24 of the Right to Information Act, 2005. Discuss its impact on transparency.
explain.who: Kerala High Court, PK Muralikrishnan, Joy Kaitharath, State Government of Kerala
explain.video_query: Kerala High Court RTI exemption VACB witness protection scheme

stories.ai_why: Relevant for judicial oversight on implementation of the Witness Protection Scheme.

points: The Kerala High Court issued notice to the State government on PIL petitions challenging the exemption of certain sections of the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) from the RTI Act.
The challenge is against a Government Order notified on October 22, 2026, which exempted the T1 and T2 sections of the VACB invoking Section 24(4) of the RTI Act.
Petitioners argued the government order discloses no reasons or objective material to prove that T1 and T2 sections constitute intelligence and security organisations.
The petition was filed by advocate PK Muralikrishnan, former legal advisor to VACB, and anti-corruption activist Joy Kaitharath.
Petitioners submitted that the mandate of these sections relates to processing corruption complaints against public servants, and excluding them violates statutory provisos.
The first proviso to Section 24(4) states that information on allegations of corruption and human rights violations shall not be excluded from RTI disclosure.
The High Court also noted that the State government is lagging in the implementation of the witness protection scheme, which involves threat assessment and protection cells.
The Court did not impose a stay on the government decision and scheduled the next hearing for November 18, 2026.

points: The Union Labour Ministry has constituted the National Social Security Boards for Unorganised Workers and Gig and Platform Workers under the Code on Social Security.

The central concern is that their centralised composition and representation gaps raise issues about inclusive decision-making and cooperative federalism.
The Board for Unorganised Sector Workers has 40 nominated members, including 7 representatives each from workers and employers, chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
The Board for Gig and Platform Workers has 22 members, including 5 representatives each from aggregators and workers, alongside 5 State Government representatives.
Both Boards primarily perform advisory and monitoring functions, while scheme notification and implementation rely on the competent government and designated agencies.
Financing frameworks can involve contributions from the Centre, States, aggregators, workers, or CSR funds, with aggregator contributions set at 1% to 2% of annual turnover.
Challenges include centralised governance, federal friction due to labour being in the Concurrent List, representation gaps, and portability difficulties for migrant workers.
Success requires inclusive representation, sustainable financing, institutional reforms, Centre-State coordination, and portable welfare entitlements.

explain.headline: ISRO Launches NVS-03 Navigation Satellite Aboard GSLV-F18 from Sriharikota
static: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), formerly IRNSS, is an autonomous regional satellite navigation system designed by ISRO to provide accurate positioning within India and up to 1,500 km beyond.

The system consists of a constellation of satellites in geostationary and geosynchronous orbits, providing Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for civilian users and Restricted Service (RS) for authorized military users.
The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is a three-stage launch vehicle with solid, liquid, and indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS) capabilities.
Atomic clocks, specifically rubidium atomic frequency standards, are crucial for satellite navigation as precise time measurement directly determines positional accuracy.
ISRO was founded in 1969 under the Department of Space to execute India's space program, with headquarters in Bengaluru and primary launch operations at Sriharikota.
explain.what: ISRO successfully launched the second-generation navigation satellite NVS-03 aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit. The mission restores NavIC to its minimum operational configuration of four satellites.
explain.why_in_news: The successful orbital injection of NVS-03 restores operational Position, Navigation, and Timing services for NavIC and strengthens infrastructure for Indian Standard Time.
explain.background: NavIC was developed by ISRO as an independent regional navigation satellite system to provide accurate positioning and timing over India and 1,500 km surrounding its borders.
significance: Restores operational redundancy to India's sovereign satellite navigation constellation, mitigating strategic vulnerabilities.
Enhances precision timing infrastructure required for the legal implementation of Indian Standard Time under the 'one nation, one time' project.
Bolsters indigenous satellite manufacturing with 80 percent of the mission budget invested into domestic Indian industries.
prelims: NavIC covers the Indian mainland and a regional area extending 1,500 km beyond its borders.
NVS-03 weighs 2,232 kg, carries an indigenous Rubidium atomic clock, and transmits across L1, L5, and S bands.
The satellite's final targeted orbital position is a Geosynchronous slot located at 32.5 degrees East.
GSLV-F18 achieved a turnaround time of 56 days between successive GSLV launches.
explain.mains: Discuss the strategic and civilian significance of the NavIC constellation for India. How does the induction of second-generation NVS satellites enhance sovereign navigation capabilities?
explain.where: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh
explain.who: ISRO, ISRO chief V Narayanan, Union MoS Jitendra Singh

points: ISRO successfully launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite aboard a GSLV rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota.
The launch was conducted to augment India's regional satellite navigation system and restore NavIC to its minimum operational configuration of four satellites.
NavIC provides sovereign Position, Navigation, and Timing services, reducing reliance on foreign systems like GPS for critical civilian and strategic needs.
The 2,232 kg satellite was injected into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit with a perigee of 170 km and an apogee of 37,023 km.
In an unprecedented safety measure to ensure propulsion reliability, ISRO flew NVS-03 with its pyrotechnic valves already open.
The satellite carries an indigenous Rubidium atomic clock and broadcasts signals across the L1, L5, and S frequency bands.
The GSLV-F18 marked the rocket's 20th flight, completed with a record turnaround time of 56 days between successive missions.
NVS-03 will maneuver into its final geosynchronous slot at 32.5 degrees East to bolster regional tracking and the 'one nation, one time' project.

explain.headline: World Bank Reports Sharp Decline in India Extreme Poverty to 2.6 Percent
static: Poverty estimation in independent India was traditionally based on minimum nutritional intake requirements, recommended by planning groups such as the Alagh Committee (1979) and Lakdawala Committee (1993).
The Tendulkar Committee (2009) shifted poverty estimation from calorie intake to uniform private household consumption expenditure across rural and urban areas, covering health and education.
The Rangarajan Committee (2014) revised methodology using an independent basket of goods, estimating poverty lines at 32 rupees for rural areas and 47 rupees for urban areas per day.

NITI Aayog publishes the National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) using National Family Health Survey (NFHS) data across three equally weighted dimensions: health, education, and standard of living.
The World Bank periodically updates international poverty lines based on Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) exchange rates to compare absolute poverty across global economies.
explain.what: According to the World Bank's October 2026 brief, India's extreme poverty fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023. Additionally, the share living below the lower-middle-income line of $4.20 per day dropped to 16.1%.
explain.why_in_news: The World Bank published its October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief highlighting India's decade-long poverty reduction and existing structural inequalities.
explain.background: Poverty measurement involves monetary and multidimensional metrics. While India previously relied on official committees like Tendulkar and Rangarajan, global agencies use international purchasing power parity thresholds.
significance: Validates the impact of large-scale social welfare programmes, food subsidies, and rural female job creation over the past decade.
Underlines that policy must now pivot from basic poverty alleviation to generating high-productivity jobs and reducing regional disparities.
Essential for UPSC questions on inclusive growth, poverty lines, wage inequality, and regional economic imbalances.
prelims: India's extreme poverty rate dropped from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023.
Population below the $4.20/day line declined from 57.7% in 2011 to 16.1% in 2023.
57% of India's poor live in a contiguous belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal.
Median earnings of the top 10% were roughly 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023.
explain.mains: While India has achieved significant success in reducing monetary poverty, persistent wage inequality and spatial concentration of poverty present major hurdles to inclusive growth. Discuss.
explain.where: India (specifically Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal belt)
explain.who: The World Bank
explain.video_query: World Bank India poverty reduction report 2026

stories.ai_why: Crucial data on India's poverty decline from the World Bank.

points: The World Bank Poverty and Equity Brief reported India's extreme poverty rate declined sharply to 2.6% in 2023 from 27.1% in 2011.
The decline was driven by robust household consumption growth, extensive expansion in employment, higher female workforce participation, and targeted government social welfare transfers.
Despite rapid monetary poverty reduction, substantial structural challenges persist around deep wage disparities, stagnant real earnings, low-productivity jobs, and rising youth unemployment.
Between 2011 and 2023, the population living below the lower-middle-income poverty threshold of 4.20 dollars per day fell from 57.7% to 16.1%.
This shift represents roughly 496 million individuals lifting themselves above the 4.20 dollars per day lower-middle-income poverty threshold over the twelve-year period.
Employment expanded by around 13.4 crore between 2017 and 2023, largely fueled by rural women entering the paid labor force.
In 2023, median earnings for the top 10% of workers were approximately 13 times higher than those of the bottom 10%.
Poverty has become heavily concentrated geographically, with around 57% of India's poor residing in a contiguous belt spanning from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal.
The World Bank projects India's lower-middle-income poverty rate will decrease further to 14.2% in 2026 and reach 12.1% by 2028.

points: The Department of Telecommunications introduced new cybersecurity requirements under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024, known as the DoT SIM Binding Rules 2027.
The rules mandate that messaging applications such as WhatsApp and Telegram must remain linked to the active SIM card of the user's registered Indian mobile number.
The primary objective is to prevent cyber fraud, online scams, and the misuse of Indian mobile numbers by criminals operating domestically or internationally.
If a user removes, replaces, or deactivates the registered SIM card, the messaging application may stop functioning until required SIM verification is completed.
The government extended the compliance deadline to December 31, 2026, with the requirements officially taking effect from January 1, 2027.
Initial rules requiring web-based sessions to log out every six hours were replaced with a risk-based logout system to terminate sessions upon detecting suspicious activity.
Platforms named in original directions include WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareShare, Josh, JioChat, and Signal, though compliance status varies.
The rules create challenges for multiple-device users, international travellers, and individuals who frequently switch SIM cards or rely on Wi-Fi without their registered SIM.

explain.headline: Nepal and Bhutan propose COP31 agenda item on mountain warming
static: The UNFCCC is an international environmental treaty adopted in 1992, aiming to prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system.
The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the supreme decision-making body of the UNFCCC, meeting annually to review climate action implementation.
The Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region is a critical global water tower spanning multiple countries, highly sensitive to climate change impacts.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assesses scientific information related to climate change, providing periodic assessment reports for policymakers.
The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 outlines targets to prevent and reduce new and existing disaster risks.
explain.what: Nepal and Bhutan have jointly submitted a formal proposal to include '1.5degC Warming in Mountains' as a supplementary provisional agenda item at COP31.
explain.why_in_news: The two Himalayan nations submitted the formal request ahead of COP31 to draw global attention to accelerating climate impacts on mountain ecosystems.
explain.background: Mountain regions face rapid warming that threatens glaciers, biodiversity, and downstream water security for billions, prompting demands for formal institutional recognition under the UNFCCC.
significance: Highlights the disproportionate vulnerability of mountain regions and upstream-downstream interdependencies in global climate negotiations.
Pushes for dedicated institutional mechanisms like a UNFCCC Work Programme on Mountain Ecosystems and equitable climate finance.
Brings regional disasters and cryospheric hazards into the formal UNFCCC policy framework.
prelims: COP31 is scheduled to be held in Antalya, Turkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026.
The proposal draws its legal foundation from the preamble and Article 4.8 of the UNFCCC.
The Bhote Koshi flash flood triggered by a glacier collapse resulted in estimated reconstruction needs of $4.7 billion in Nepal.
Mountain regions cover nearly a quarter of the Earth's surface and support about 15 percent of the global population.
explain.mains: Discuss the significance of including mountain-specific agenda items in global climate negotiations such as the UNFCCC COP, keeping in view the vulnerabilities of the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

stories.ai_why: Himalayan nations collaborating on climate agenda for COP summits matters for IR and environment.

points: Nepal and Bhutan jointly proposed a dedicated agenda item titled '1.5degC Warming in Mountains' for COP31 of the UNFCCC.
The formal submission was addressed to the COP president, incoming COP president, and the executive secretary of the UNFCCC.
The proposal warns that accelerated warming in regions like the Hindu Kush Himalaya threatens glaciers, water security, and livelihoods.
Mountain ecosystems supply freshwater to over two billion people across Asia and support nearly a quarter of the Earth's surface.
The legal foundation for the proposal is drawn from the preamble and Article 4.8 of the UNFCCC, citing specific ecosystem vulnerabilities.
The countries propose four major areas: advancing scientific understanding of overshoot, an annual high-level dialogue, a dedicated work programme, and integrating priorities into finance.
Recent disasters such as the 2026 Bhote Koshi catastrophe highlight the severe economic and infrastructure vulnerabilities faced by mountain nations.
